text:
Good morning, everybody. I declare open this hearing of the Senate Finance and Public Administration Legislation Committee into the 2026-27 supplementary budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders past and present and extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people here today.

The committee has set Thursday 5 November 2026 as the date by which senators are to submit written questions on notice, and Thursday 17 December 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will begin with the parliamentary departments, followed by the Prime Minister and Cabinet portfolio, as listed on today's program. Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session, and this includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance for questions at estimates hearings: any question going to the operation or financial position of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted.

Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

I remind senators of their obligation under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect, and, as is my usual practice, I have provided copies of that code in the room for people's reference.

Before we begin, I would like to on behalf of the committee send our thoughts to our colleague the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines, and also to her family, her team and her community as she continues to recover in hospital. The attack against Dr Haines on Monday last week was a horrendous incident and quite horrific, and I know that we have all come back to this place in some level of distress and shock. Dr Haines is much loved as a colleague here and as a strong advocate for her community and for democracy in general. Contributions will be made in the House of Representatives this morning from 10 am, and the committee will suspend at 9.50 to enable members to attend and pay their respects. I know that investigations are underway by the Victorian police, by the AFP and by ASIO, and I ask senators to please be mindful of this during these hearings.

Dr Haines is known to all of us as a person of extreme integrity and someone who conducts public debate in a robust but respectful manner. As chair I will be taking this spirit on board with some gusto today, and I have no doubt that my fellow senators will join me in paying that respect to Dr Haines.

Some of my staff have worked closely with Dr Haines, particularly in joint-committee settings. Most recently, she's the deputy chair of the joint committee overseeing the National Anti-Corruption Commission. My staff and the many, many staff in the House of Representatives who have worked closely with her have been profoundly affected by these events. The circumstances of the incident are deeply unsettling and have been felt right across the parliamentary community. The safety of and support for all participants in parliamentary and public life is of paramount importance as we navigate the aftermath of these events. I wanted to put that on the record on behalf of my staff.

As has been foreshadowed, I hope for this to be my last estimates! I hope you take that in the spirit in which it's intended. Since 1999, the position of the Clerk of the Senate has been a position appointed by the president of the day after consultation with senators for a single, non-renewable 10-year term. That 10 years expires on 8 March next year, so theoretically I could sneak in one more round of estimates. I'm subject to the compulsory powers of this committee, and I'm tempted, because 8 March is Canberra Day, and ending your career on the Canberra Day public holiday would surely be a highlight, but it would be my intention, with the President's blessing, because she has to approve my leave, to begin a period of leave from the end of January next year. I wanted to express my thanks to senators and to their staff for the way that they've engaged with me and my team over my tenure as Clerk and for putting the faith in me and my team to provide the advice and support that we're here to provide so that you can participate in the proceedings of the Senate and its committees. I do deeply thank senators for the trust that they have expressed in me over that time and for mostly engaging in a positive spirit, even in this room.

I also want to thank my staff. The staff of the Senate department are amazing, not just the ones in the room today. They're a dedicated, committed, engaged, professional and profoundly talented bunch of people, and it's been an absolute honour to lead them these last 10 years and, more broadly, to have been part of the team for 35 years by the time I walk out the door. That's long enough, I think. Even if that single 10-year term wasn't there, I suspect I would be waltzing out the door sometime next year. Thank you to this committee for allowing me to make this statement. Thank you for your engagement with me over the years. Thank you to senators and their staff more broadly and the occasional member of the House of Representatives who's stumbled onto the pink carpet for advice. In particular, thank you to my staff for the faith that they have placed in me. Thank you, Chair.

text: I'm going to start, if I may, with some pretty regular questions that I've been asking you now for some time—questions, ironically, about questions—just to make it clear for senators and witnesses and the government about how questions should be treated as part of the estimates proceedings. In relation to questions on notice, Clerk, can you please tell me the difference between a question that might be taken verbally on notice in a hearing and a question on notice provided to a witness in writing?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: There's little difference in relation to how such questions should be treated. Committees set dates for questions to be asked and questions to be answered, and the expectation is that questions that are taken on notice during a hearing and questions that are placed on notice in writing after a hearing should be answered with the same alacrity and to the same timelines. There's no reason to treat one type of question any differently to another.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Terrific. In terms of the number of questions that may be taken on notice by a witness, they are unlimited in their discretion to take a question on notice—is that correct?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Well, yes, except that senators and the Senate more broadly expect that witnesses who come to give evidence at estimates should be well prepared, so it should be unnecessary to take questions on notice where public servants are prepared and aware of the sorts of questions that might be asked. But there is a range of reasons why people might need to take questions on notice, either because they don't have the information to hand, it goes to a level of detail that isn't immediately available to them, or there might be considerations as to whether a public interest immunity claim might need to be made in relation to some of that information. But procedurally, there's no limit to the number of questions that can be taken on notice or placed on notice, with the caveat that there is an expectation that officials coming before hearings will be well prepared.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: And if a Senator has given a department advance notice that it will be asking questions about a particular topic, there would be an expectation that they would not just become well prepared but also that they wouldn't need to take questions on notice if that were the case.

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I think that's broadly right. There will always be levels of detail that people won't have, or people aren't going to know what aspects of some questions that senators are going to go to. Of course, it depends on the period of notice. It can take a little while to put together a public interest immunity claim and think about all the different consequences, so there will always be those situations.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Are there any limitations on the number of questions that can be placed on notice by Senator?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: There are no procedural limitations. I think I've said before there's an opportunity cost involved, though, in asking more and more questions, in that Public Service departments and agencies have limited resources themselves. An official who is preparing answers to questions on notice isn't doing something else that they might have as part of their duties. I sometimes worry that the answers to questions that go to more profound matters might get delayed or lost in the course of people answering more formulaic questions. We've seen in the Senate, from time to time, senators needing to move orders for the production of documents to get answers that they might have expected at estimates, and a response saying, 'There are so many questions asked of a particular department, that it necessarily leads to delays.' It would be a shame to clog up a system that is meant to be, and has for many years, been the jewel in the accountability crown.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text:
I want to thank you very much for tabling the advertisement that's gone out for expressions of interest in the Clerk's position. We did that during your break.

I want to ask just one last round of questions to the Clerk before I hand over to my colleague. I would be remiss not to do this, considering this is your last Senate estimates, Mr Pye. At the last hearings, you spoke to us about the narrowing of the application of privilege and particularly the submissions to the Senate Committee on Privileges and part of the 189th report from the AG's Department and the Department of Parliamentary Services. I'm wondering whether we can use this opportunity to talk to the two aspects of privilege that you mentioned before and how they can be confused or incorrectly applied in a narrow way.

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Certainly. The issue that we that we were discussing on the last occasion went to. The aspect of privilege around the protection that it gives to proceedings in parliament and the protection that it gives to the duties of senators as senators. There is sometimes a tendency for people to assume that the protection of parliamentary material before the court is the beginning and end of the protections afforded by parliamentary privilege. We were specifically talking about the extension of that protection into areas beyond the courts and the experience that the parliament has had in relation to the execution of search warrants, which may involve privilege and may involve potentially privileged materials, and the right of senators, their staff and other participants in parliamentary proceedings to make a claim of privilege in relation to material that someone might be seeking to seize or access under a statutory power. The Senate's position, which is well established now, that claims of privilege over such material must be determined by the Senate—
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: By the senator?

agency: Department of the Senate
text:
By the Senate itself. But the trigger for that is usually a Senator saying: 'Hold on. You're exercising a statutory power in relation to material that I hold, material that has been given to me or material that I am using for proceedings. I make a claim of privilege over that.' That triggers a process for the quarantining of the material, usually with the clerk of the relevant house, and the question to be referred to the Senate Standing Committee of Privileges for investigation as to whether the material warrants protection under privilege. It's that aspect of privilege that was being a little bit in the submissions that you referred to from the Department of Parliamentary Services and the Attorney-General's Department. That protection is something that the Senate has declared. In the back of the standing orders there's a resolution—No. 38(b), I think it is; people are checking for me. These are all details that will fall out of my head in three months time, I suspect! But that is a resolution that the Senate passed in 2018 to declare and reinforce—38(a). There you go; it's already fallen out of my head. It was to declare and reinforce that one of the purposes of privilege is to protect parliamentary material against incursion by executive agencies, or people exercising statutory search-and-seizure powers or exercising covert statutory powers to access material that might be on a server or something like that.

In all of those circumstances, privilege has probably not been abrogated by the statute under which the powers are given. Almost all of the statutes either don't mention it at all, in which case you can only narrow privilege by an express statutory provision to that effect—if you don't mention it. What is more common is for the act that establishes the search-and-seizure and access powers—they will commonly say, 'This does not abrogate privilege.' So, in all of those circumstances, privilege obtains, and the declaration in continuing resolution No. 38A, which was made in December of 2018, is to say that one of the purposes of privilege is to guard against incursion of that material. It doesn't mean the material is protected to an infinite degree. What it means is that the question of the protection of the material becomes a question for the Senate. In the past—in the Conroy matter in 2016 and in another matter involving the Legal and Constitutional Affairs References Committee in around 2018—the process that was followed was for the question to be put by the Senate before the privileges committee and the privileges committee to recommend, as it did in both of those cases, that the material be withheld from the investigators and returned to the senator involved, because it was beyond the scope of the seizure powers to seize that material once it was analysed by the Senate.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Okay. Thank you. It's very helpful, I think, to reiterate that. I've just got two more lines of questioning, and then I'll turn the call over to my colleague here. That's correct?

agency: Department of the Senate

I met with the Secretary of the DPS and corresponded with her, and we engaged also with the Clerk of the House of Representatives, to put together a draft of those principles. I understand the draft went to the Senate privileges committee and also to the House privileges committee. I understand there's been some further work within that committee which has not been reported. You will know the status of that aspect of it, but my understanding was that the committee and the Department of Parliamentary Services were getting close to agreement. But I presume there'll need to be a further meeting of the Senate committee in the next sittings, to finalise that work.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Is it expected that that process will be complete before your retirement?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I believe so. I would be very surprised—and the President has met with the chair of the privileges committee on that matter as well.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: That's good.

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I think all indications are that it's close to finalisation.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: How is the department managing or handling matters of privilege that might be covered by those principles while they're in development?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: To some degree, this is a question for the Department of Parliamentary Services, but the—
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Yes, I will be asking them.

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I suspected you would—hello, Jaala. The department itself prepared a temporary protocol at the end of last year, ahead of the privileges committee reporting. I understand that that is what's being applied. witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: With regard to the application of parliamentary privilege within the context of a committee hearing or a proceeding, does a witness have the capacity to determine the manner of the publication of their testimony?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: No. That's a matter for committees within the powers that are delegated to them by the Senate and by the House. Committees are responsible for the publication of their proceedings and the integrity of their proceedings, subject, as I say, only to any guidance or rules that the Senate applies to their work.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Obviously, you're aware that recently a public servant appeared before a committee and stated that public servants didn't consent to the use of their images on social media. You provided some advice on that matter—is that correct?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I provided some advice to the committee at that stage, yes. I think it was referred to by the chair and another member of that committee as the hearing then progressed.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: What was that advice?

agency: Department of the Senate
text:
Simply that it's absolutely not something that a witness can do and that there are well-established paths for witnesses, potential witnesses and other people who are engaging with the work of committees or giving evidence or making submissions to committees—there are well-trodden paths for people to raise these matters through the secretariats or with the committees themselves or to raise matters with the Senate department through our staff who are responsible for the management of committees.

This is not to minimise the fact that there are some people who have been very bruised by their experiences before Senate and House committees and the treatment of footage that has come out of those. On the weekend I was looking at some footage and some commentary underneath the footage on social media. I won't refer to the hearing. It wasn't something that was posted by a senator; it was posted by someone who's obviously got it from the web feed, and the commentary underneath it was horrendous. The reflections on the witness were atrocious—exactly the sort of thing that we would hope that the code of conduct, for instance, in this place and the behavioural codes seek to guard against. So I understand that people have been bruised and really deeply affected by some of these issues. But it was profoundly unhelpful, I thought on the day, for the matter to be raised in that way without any notice to anybody, not through the secretariat, not to the chair and not to other members of the committee. The Secretaries Board had raised the matter in a submission to the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Parliamentary Standards. That submission had not been published—it had been received but it had not been published. No-one here had any notice of the matters that the witness was going to, and I just thought that it was not a useful way to introduce a discussion of something that is going to be a difficult discussion. It's going to require a lot of sensitivity and ingenuity. In trying to clean up the conduct associated with the way in which social media clips are dealt with, we need to remind ourselves that the accountability that is involved in these processes and the scrutiny, particularly in that case, of a contested government policy can't be thrown out in these issues. That needs to be something that is given a great deal of weight.

I've reflected elsewhere—and I don't want to get ahead of the work of that committee—that the submission from the Secretaries Board does identify that these are matters for the parliament and its members and committees to determine, and that it is a process of finding ways to improve proceedings and improve the down-flow effects, I guess, of proceedings with great respect for the work of the committees, the work of senators and members and the importance of ensuring that matters are properly dealt with by the parliament and not by way of other people purporting to rein in the activities of the Senate and its committees.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I will just draw everyone's attention to the fact that we are running considerably behind schedule, just for those waiting to appear. Senator McGrath.

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Clerk, if I read it correctly, the annual report records an operating deficit of $310,000 for 2025-26 compared with a profit of just over $1 million in the previous financial year. Is that correct?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I think that's correct, yes.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Are you able to expand on the principal reasons for the deterioration in the department's financial position?

agency: Department of the Senate
text:
I suppose I can. A thing that I've drawn attention to throughout my time as Clerk is the fact that the levels of legislative and committee activity tend to run in a relatively predictable way through the parliamentary cycle. In the first year of a parliament it takes a little while for the activity to ramp up. We've had some exceptions—four years ago, the Senate decided it would start on 2 July, so activity ramped up a bit more quickly—but this past year was a little bit more typical. So it takes a little while for business to ramp up. The second year is usually the busiest and the third year is often slightly less expensive, in that there's a hiatus in some legislative and committee activity as we go to the election.

So the 2024-25 result, which is that surplus, reflects the fact that legislative activity slowed down and committee activity slowed down from March and April as we went to the election period. Last year, 2025-26, we thought we were on track for a break-even position and then, quite late in the period, we were asked to recalculate how we calculate our leave liabilities, and there was some bond rate movements. So, what we thought was going—
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Could you expand on that please?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I probably can't, but I could ask John to expand.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: To try to explain it in easy terms, the way that the liability is presented shows the discounted cost; it's not the actual real nominal cost. It's been discounted using various factors such as bond rates and those sorts of things. It's meant to represent the time value of money—the amount that we have to purport based on probabilities of people taking their leave or achieving their long-service leave balance, because after 10 years you accrue it; the discount factors in there; and also a growth rate for salaries. So those sorts of things at the end of the year tend to be a last-minute adjustment at the end of the financial statements. And this year, because of the movements in bond rates and the like and a change to the calculation basis, it pushed us over for the year. It's not even a cash deficit; it's just an accounting deficit in the books.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I told you I probably couldn't expand on it.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: We're pretty much on track otherwise.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: So in the first year of new parliament there's often more activity than the last year of the previous parliament. So that explains the difference between the surplus the prior year and the almost-break-even-but-not-quite position that we achieved in 2025-26.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: You also mentioned that the report refers to the timing of recruitment as a factor in managing expenditure. Were any positions deliberately left vacant or recruitment processes delayed for budgetary reasons?

agency: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I just have one other quick block of questions in relation to the Parliamentary Education Office. The annual report states that the department sought additional funding to expand the Parliamentary Education Office's online outreach activities. Is that correct?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: That is correct, yes.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: How much additional funding was requested?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I think it was in the order of $1.5 million per annum for four years.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: What specific activities would the additional funding have supported?

agency: Department of the Senate
text:
There are a couple of aspects to that. Some of it was online outreach and some of it was physical outreach. These were matters that were the subject of recommendations by the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters in its report on civics education. The department, in seeking funds, was responding to those recommendations as well as a recommendation of the PEO advisory board. The advisory board is co-chaired by the Deputy President of the Senate and the Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, with membership drawn from both houses and from across different parties.

During COVID, the PEO pivoted pretty quickly to presenting online role-play sessions and supplementing its website material with interactive video-link sessions. Post-COVID, we pivoted back to having 90,000 students come into the building as the main pathway for delivering our education role-play, but there remained a demand for online activities as well. We really were only funded for one or the other. We have managed to continue the process of the online role-play, but we were looking to expand that work and the physical outreach programs that we undertake. That involves the PEO, sometimes in collaboration with, for instance, the Electoral Commission, going out and setting up in a school somewhere. Schools from the local region then come along to get an equivalent experience that they would be able to get by coming to the Senate.

There's an additional aspect of that, which is the teacher training aspect of that work. We were seeking to expand that work; that's what the funding bid was for. It aligned with some thinking that the Department of Education had, I think, on another possible budget bid that I don't believe went ahead. But that was the intention.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: So, in short, the unsuccessful funding increase has prevented the Parliamentary Education Office from expanding both its online programs and its in-person programs?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Its in-person outreach, so the physical outreach program—I think we do two trips a year. We wanted to double that to four, and we wanted to have a more dedicated online role-play session as well. The program that people come to Canberra to do is a fantastic program. It's really well regarded. I attended one quite recently. The educators are brilliant, and the kids really get engaged with it. It's a fantastic thing. But the truth is that kids from low-socioeconomic schools are unlikely to get to Canberra—much less likely to get to Canberra. Kids from the remote regions are much less likely to come to Canberra. So, in line with the recommendations of the electoral matters committee, we were hoping to be able to supplement those programs, add that teacher-training element of it and expand the education offerings in those ways.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text:
President, considering the funding increase came about through effectively a recommendation of the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters, were you given any reason by the government as to why the bid was not successful?

The President: No, and they are really questions for government. I supported the bid. I've seen the work. I happened to be in Karratha when they were presenting an outside presentation to three schools. It was really good. I was very impressed. I participated. So I think it's—

agency: Department of the Senate
text:
But I suppose my question is: Did they tell you why? Did they say, 'Come back next year'? Did they say, 'Look, we just don't have the money'? Was there a reason why it wasn't approved? I think we all would agree that civics education is so important, and it's—

The President: Senator McGrath, you've been in government. You know how these processes work. We're not usually given a reason. The bid went up. Those are questions for government.

agency: Department of the Senate
text: But I do think, Senator, it's an aspect of our work that is so important, and I think a budget bid along those lines is well worth revisiting.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Good. So you intend to seek the funding again in the next budget?

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I won't be seeking anything in the next budget, but I'm sure that my successor and my senior colleagues will be weighing up the pros and cons of going ahead.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Thank you. I'm good, thank you, Chair.

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Any further questions? Excellent. Thank you so much for your time. I'm reluctant to let you go, Mr Pye!

agency: Department of the Senate
text:
Don't be, Chair.

The President: Join the club!
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: We've tried to keep you here as long as we can this morning, but we will reserve our right to recall you in February, should we feel the urge. I'm just joking. Thank you so much. Thank you for everything that you do for this parliament and have done for so long. We really are going to miss you.

agency: Department of the Senate
text: Thank you, Chair.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Department of the Senate
text: I now ask the Parliamentary Budget Office to come to the table.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Welcome, Ms Reinhardt and your colleagues, various officers of the Parliamentary Budget Office. Would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Chair, I would like to make a very short opening statement.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Excellent. Please go right ahead.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text:
Good morning, Chair, Deputy Chair and members of the committee, and thank you for the opportunity to make a brief opening statement. First, on behalf of the PBO staff, I want to express our deep sadness following the attack on Helen Haines and extend our support to her family, herself and her staff. We recognise that Dr Haines played an important role in parliamentary accountability and transparency, and we recognise her commitment to the role of the PBO as the only independent member to have all her commitments costed in the last two election commitments reports. In our daily work with parliamentarians, we see their dedication to serving Australia, and we also want to take this opportunity to acknowledge that and how much members and senators commit to their work.

The PBO recently released our 2025-26 annual report. It shows demand for our services remains high. The number of requests received is 20 per cent higher than at the same stage of the 47th Parliament. Looking further back, both demand and output have tripled since 2019-20, which is the equivalent parliamentary period in the 46th Parliament. To manage our workload, we work closely with parties and parliamentarians to understand their priorities, keep them informed of progress and direct our resources to urgent requests. This sometimes means placing other requests on hold so that time-sensitive work can proceed. We aim to be transparent and fair in managing these priorities while maintaining confidentiality. We will continue to pursue efficiencies without compromising the quality, independence or confidentiality of our advice.

We are also making good progress on implementing the recommendations of the independent review of the PBO. The review was commissioned by the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit and completed in March this year. The review found the PBO is performing well and is held in high regard, while identifying practical opportunities to improve our engagement, transparency and impact. We provided our formal response to the JCPAA on 31 August this year and accepted all recommendations directed to the PBO. Actions already taken or underway include clearer communication with requesters and stronger engagement with parties. They also include the introduction of policy costing analysis work, a more accessible budget snapshot and the release of our guide to the 2026 Intergenerational report. During the remainder of this financial year, we'll continue to implement the recommendations of the review.

Finally, I would like to note the PBO's 2026 APS census results, where 95 per cent of staff participated, and the results indicate a highly engaged and purpose driven organisation. Staff understand and support the PBO's purpose and objectives. They understand how their roles contribute to outcomes for parliament. At the same time, they reported high workloads, competing priorities and tight timeframes, reflecting the strong demand for our services. Ensuring priorities are clear and workloads remain sustainable will continue to be an important focus of the leadership team, and I would like to acknowledge the professionalism, commitment and sustained effort of PBO staff. Thank you. We welcome questions.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Thank you very much. We'll go to Senator McGrath.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Thank you for the work that you and your team do. I just want to allow you to do a bit of advertising, in a way. Can you confirm that every senator and MP elected to the Australian parliament has access to the PBO to have their policies costed, regardless of their party affiliation or status?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: That's correct.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: So you can cost policies from parties as well as independent senators and members.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: That is correct.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: So if a member or senator has said that they do not have access to your services, that is a factually incorrect statement.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: That is a factually incorrect statement.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: You also run outreach programs about the services of the PBO. I think I recall seeing lots of emails from your team. Is that correct? It is a good thing, by the way.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: We do a lot of outreach. We also offer to do budget briefings and engagement with both members and senators but also their staff, if staff are after information on budgets and how the budget works or how to read the budget. It is the case that in the election commitment report it is a different approach, in that designated parties—that is, parties with five or more members going into caretaker—are included in our election commitments report. That is, we are required under legislation to report on their commitments. For independents or parties with fewer than five members, they can, as Dr Haines did, elect to be part of that election commitments report.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Moving on, your latest annual report records a just over $1 million asset write-off associated with your relocation to West Block. Is that correct?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: That's correct. Essentially, when we moved, there were a number of things that we couldn't take with us. Desks and things like that were organised for us in West Block, and there were things that we had to leave behind in the accommodation here. I will try and articulate what they are. They include cables in the wall. All of that comes to $1 million, unfortunately.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Can you remind me—who made the decision to relocate you from within Parliament House to West Block?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: We work with the Department of Parliamentary Services, and, as you're aware, they have to do renovations to the building, given the age of the building, and we worked with them about moving to West Block. Everyone recognises it's not ideal for us to be outside the parliament. We are quite close. We still have an office up here where we can bring people up during sitting periods, and we do come up a lot, as needed, to meet with parliamentarians and advisers.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Is the relocation intended to be permanent?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text:
It's a temporary relocation, and one of the recommendations of the independent review was that there be reporting on what the plans were for us to relocate back to Parliament House.

The President: Senator McGrath, it's been my very firm view that PBO return to this place.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text:
Do we have a date, President, at all?

The President: Ms Reinhardt might know better than me, or it's perhaps a question for DPS.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: I think it is a question for DPS. We don't have a date at this point.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Okay. To DPS listening: could you have that answer ready, please. I've got some other questions I can put on notice in relation to that. Can I go to staffing, please. Can you give me an update on the current number of PBO staff and where they are located—because you mentioned you still have a small footprint here.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Yes. We have an office here which we populate with around four staff for each sitting period. We have staff in West Block together otherwise, because we're a relatively small organisation. We're currently sitting at around 48 ASL, but we keep them all together in West Block. We do have one staff member who works out of Brisbane. That's an unusual circumstance where someone has moved away from Canberra and we have kept him working for the organisation at the moment. But, otherwise, we're all in West Block.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Has your overall staffing reduced in the last financial year?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Each year that an election is expected, we receive half a million dollars in addition to our standard budget. That's not indexed. Since 2012, that's been the election uplift. Other than that, our annual appropriation is indexed by, I think, 3.38 per cent a year, staffing wages go up by 3.7 per cent a year and there's an efficiency dividend of one per cent a year. So, if you add all those numbers up, that's a slight decrease over time.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: How would you characterise the PBO's current workload? Has your office been busier in this parliament at this time compared to, say, in the previous parliament at this time?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Yes. In the last financial year, we had 20 per cent more costing requests. They're pretty raw numbers because often it just comes down to how extensive those requests are. One costing request is not the same as another. I'd say it's pretty consistent with the previous parliament, but that was a very heavy workload. PBO is in high demand, and we're managing within that and we are working closely with parties and parliamentarians to make sure we're delivering the highest-priority costings work.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Has the increased demand placed pressure on your existing staff and resources?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: They say it has, according to the census. We are trying to work to make sure everyone's really clear on priorities and what needs to get done and what we're able to achieve within our resources.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Are you adequately resourced by the government to meet the current demand for PBO services?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: We have a good level of resource to work within. I would say that it would be no surprise that there are a number of costings that are sitting on the books. I think it's currently 76 that are sitting on the books that we're still working through. So there's always a stock, and that stock gets higher over the parliamentary cycle. I do expect the demand will go up over the next two years leading towards an election.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: You mentioned the extra half a million dollars you receive in an election year. Considering what you just said, in relation to that answer, then you expect it to increase in the lead-up over the next two years.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: That's been the consistent picture since 2012 when we were established.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Will the PBO seek additional funding?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: We may well, we have in the last two budgets. Again, that's been on the record, and we've shared that with the JCPAA, which is the committee we work directly to, or are accountable to, under the legislation.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: But just for those listening, who may may not sit on that committee or watch its proceedings, have you sought additional funding previously. And has that funding been approved?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: No, but budgets are tight. We know that. As the PBO, it's our job to recognise that budgets are also tight.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Considering the brilliant work you and your team do for the work of this parliament, especially non-government senators, it would be a concern if your work is being restrained because of a lack of sufficient financial resources. I've received reports that some parliamentary officers are being advised it could take up to three months to complete a policy costing. You touched upon it in a previous answer. Is this because of a resourcing issue?

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Without knowing the particular case at hand, probably. But then I would also say that some of our costing requests are extremely complex, particularly at this stage in the parliamentary cycle, as parties and parliamentarians are working out how their policies look, and what they would like to take to an election. So it can also be a function of what's being costed.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: This is a Dorothy Dixer, so you'll probably answer it very appropriately. Would additional resources help you reach your performance target of 15 business days or fewer in relation to—

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of the Senate

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text:
It would. I do have further questions, but I'll put them on notice. Thank you and thank you to your team for the brilliant work that you do.

The President: Senator McGrath, I am advised that I did receive a response from the finance minister in relation to the Parliamentary Education Office's unsuccessful bid. I'll table that.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: Thank you.

agency: Parliamentary Budget Office
text: I believe there are no further questions, so thank you very much to the PBO for coming and joining us. We do appreciate your time.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Welcome to Ms Jaala Hinchcliffe, the Secretary, and other officers of the Department of Parliamentary Services. Welcome to Ms Jacqui Curtis, the Parliamentary Service Commissioner. Thank you for your patience. I know we're running a little late. Would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
I just have a few quick remarks to make, if that's okay, Chair. I'm conscious of time. I would like to add to the words of my parliamentary department colleagues, Ms Reinhardt and Mr Pye and express the deep sadness of the Department of Parliamentary Services in relation to the attack on Dr Helen Haines and to express that our thoughts and prayers are with her and her family. Our role as the Department of Parliamentary Services is to provide services to parliamentarians and to parliamentary departments to support our great Australian democracy, and we have felt shocked and saddened by the events of last week.

I'd also like to just quickly express my gratitude for the great work of our outgoing clerk, Mr Pye. I have known the Clerk for many, many years and worked with him when he was the Deputy Clerk and now with him as the Clerk. I often say that there is nowhere else that has the collegiality that is shown in the Parliamentary Service, and that is because the four Parliamentary Service departments work so closely together to provide services to parliament and to parliamentarians. Mr Pye has been a great friend and a great source of advice. He will be well missed by all of us. I pass on our congratulations from DPS on his imminent retirement. Thank you, Chair.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Thank you very much. Ms Curtis, would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Thank you. I would just like to concur with my colleague Jaala Hinchcliffe about the condolences and the regrettable circumstances that have befallen Helen Haines and just say that we across the service are thinking of her and her family. That's all I have to say.
witness_organisation: Parliamentary Service Commissioner

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Thank you very much, and a warm welcome to you. We will go to Senator Hume.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: I have some questions following up on the last Senate estimates meeting, where we discussed the Senate Standing Committee of Privileges' 189th report. Ms Hinchcliffe, have the Presiding Officers and both clerks settled the draft principles that are required by recommendation 1 of that report?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Yes. As was noted in the evidence that was just given by the Clerk during his hearing, I worked together with both the clerks to draft a set of principles, as was set out in the recommendations from the committee. That then went to the Presiding Officers for them to review. I then wrote to both of the privileges committees on 11 August to provide them a copy of the draft statement. I then received correspondence from both of the house privileges committees in relation to that, including a letter from the Senate privileges committee on 15 September. I met with the chair on 14 October, when we discussed some slight amendments to the draft that the Senate committee sent back, which I understand will be considered by the Senate committee. I hope that this will be able to be finalised this year.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Right. So we're not quite at recommendation 2, which is the privileges committee's approval of the principles, yet?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: That's right.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Okay. Terrific. Can you tell me what the substantive issues that remain are and also what interim rule applies while we're waiting for that confirmation?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Well, the statement of principles goes to principles such as that, when there is a request from a third party to DPS to provide information in relation to a parliamentarian or that might include parliamentarian data, where that is provided through a compulsory power, we will work through the MOU processes that are already in place and, where there is no MOU process in place, we will discuss with the clerks, or ask the agency that is issuing the compulsory power on us to speak to the clerks about, a process to ensure that parliamentary privilege is protected. I note that at the moment the IPSC is still working on an MOU, so there are still agencies that might provide us with a notice that don't have an MOU in place. Where there is not a compulsory power that is issued on us by a third party that is still looking for information that relates to a parliamentarian, DPS will only provide that information with the consent of the parliamentarian. Then when DPS is doing work in relation to our own staff and looking at our own records, that will comply with the procedures that we put in place on 2 January, which are called 'Procedure for dealing with requests for DPS employee data that might contain parliamentarian data'.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Which divisions or investigators or outside counsel or cloud providers or forensic contractors are covered? And are there explicit contractual obligations for those?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: This relates to how DPS will deal with requests for data that come to us. So it applies to—
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Everybody.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: everybody. And, as the Clerk suggested in his evidence, of course DPS is not the only parliamentary department that holds parliamentarian data. And we have been particularly minded as to how these principles could be applied across the parliamentary departments.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: For information that's potentially engaging parliamentary privilege, who is it that authorises preservation, search, bulk extraction, transfer and review? Is it independently recorded? And who authorises that?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Under the MOUs there is a process set out, which is similar for each of them, which goes to a compulsory power being issued either on a parliamentarian or on a third party such as DPS. When that occurs there is then a process that is set out in the MOUs about the quarantining of data. For example, in the NACC MOU there are provisions for there to be an independent part of the NACC that is then doing searches before it goes to the investigator so that, if any parliamentary data is found or any data that could go to parliamentary privilege, that can be quarantined from the investigation or it can be referred back to the clerks and the House for advice should the investigation agency want to use it.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Is there an audit trail that shows who accesses any extracted data and whether copies are made?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: That would be a question for the agencies who have—
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: That's the individual agencies?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Yes, that's right. And, again, I'm being cautious here, so I have spoken about just the NACC MOU, because I have knowledge of both the NACC and the AFP MOU because of previous engagements. To understand how they work in practice, from the agencies' perspectives, is a question for the NACC and the AFP.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Recommendation 3 is about induction and annual mandatory training, and I wonder whether the induction and mandatory training have been updated in accordance with—

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: The principles haven't been finalised yet—
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: So you can't do one for the other.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: But, as I gave in evidence at last estimates, every month—and a big shout-out to the serjeant and the usher for this—they hold parliamentary privilege training, which DPS staff are invited to go to. We will have 11 sessions this year. The next session—and this is a call-out to DPS staff—is on 4 November. When I looked late last week, there were only 12 seats available. So DPS staff, if you haven't been, you need to get yourself onto that. We have made it mandatory for new staff on induction to got to parliamentary privilege training. We'll also, once the principles have been finalised, work with the usher and the serjeant in terms of that training. We're also looking at how we can work on some online training, as a refresh. I also mentioned that we do SES training, which is training just for our SES cohort. Thank you, again, to the deputy clerks, who came on 5 August to train all of our SES and do an update to our parliamentary privilege training.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: I suppose it may be early to ask this, but I will be asking for an understanding of the completion rates—

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Of course.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: particularly by seniority and contractor class, when that has been done. I should ask: have you done the training? I suppose I should ask whether both of you have done the training that, specifically, we're talking about now.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: We both went to the DPS training on 5 August, and I've been to many training sessions, including training that I had the deputy clerks come and take when I was there, when we were getting ready to move into the NACC.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Okay. Can you tell me what any departures have been from the draft to the final principle since 12 May. Have they been significant?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: The principles didn't refer to the procedures that we put in place on 2 January, so we're making sure that those procedures are mentioned in there. We've also talked about some of the additions in there, including the level of authorisation and whether that should be left to the accountable authority to decide, given that these principles should be able to be applied across parliamentary departments. I am conscious that I have got more staff at a higher level than the other parliamentary departments, so there's been a discussion about that as well.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Alright. On notice, could you please give the committee an aggregate count and—actually, look, don't worry about that one. I'll come back to that. I'm probably jumping the gun a bit. I want to ask about the department's cybersecurity, if I can.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Obviously, you're well aware of the very well-publicised incident involving Services Australia. However, I'm interested to know whether you're aware that this was an AI agent that accessed information that was not secured appropriately, and I want to understand whether the department has undertaken any work to identify information that is similarly not secured from an approach by an AI agent in your department.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
Good morning, Senator. I'm going to ask Mr Mike Webb to join us at the table in case you are after more technical details. But the one thing that the department has been focused on to a very high extent over the course of the last 12 months is as we have recognised to this committee and in other submissions. The department recognised that the operations of the parliamentary computer network needed to be uplifted. During the course of the last 12 months, the department has also been the subject of a very beneficial review by the Australian National Audit Office into cybersecurity and information management. As a result of that, the department was successful in the budget round in receiving funding to be able to uplift information across the PCN, and that's in the—Mike always laughs at me with this because I should know the acronym and I don't—the PICR, Parliamentary Information and Cyber Resilience, program. As part of that, that is going through a comprehensive review of the matters and details systems that we operate on the PCN and undertaking uplift across them all.

I think it is also fair to say, though, that it is a very dynamic environment when it comes to cybersecurity. Everyone across the room and everyone that sits in our ICT area is very mindful that it is a brave new world and there are vulnerabilities being exploited at every opportunity. DPS has got a very strong approach to cybersecurity, and we are taking it very seriously, as evidenced by the uplift work that we are undertaking. To date, while we have had some impacts that have flown through, the majority of our work has actually shown improvements in the fundamental operating basis of our system, and that will continue to improve.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: I've got some more questions about this.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: If you're going to stick with the same subject, I will give you a few more minutes, and then I'll rotate the call.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
I'm acutely conscious of that ANAO report, which was titled Management of cyber security in the Department of Parliamentary Services. It concluded that the department's cybersecurity was only 'partly effective'. It outlined:

The Department of Parliamentary Services had a partly effective baseline of essential cyber security strategies. The Essential Eight cyber security strategies had not been fully implemented in accordance with the requirements of the Protective Security Policy Framework, and compensating controls were not sufficiently effective to mitigate the full extent of risk.

Now, that sounds terrifying to me. Can we first just establish that it would be fair to say that the parliamentary computing network would be a very high-value target for malicious actors. That's correct.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: I think it'd be very fair to say that any system that's operated by any government agency that holds wholesale data on people, policies, program, budget or funding would be a high-value target, and of course that would include the PCN.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: First of all, that finding of 'partly effective', I'm assuming, is something that is of great concern to you.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: It is. As we recognised prior to the ANAO audit, by work that had been undertaken by the department, as we outlined to the committee and in other submissions, the PCN was not fit for purpose, and for that reason we have been successful in obtaining funding to be able to do a multi-year uplift program, which is now well underway.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
That report, and the quote that I just gave you, said:

… compensating controls were not sufficiently effective to mitigate the full extent of risk.

What does 'the full extent of the risk' mean?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: I'll take that one. Essentially what that's referring to is that under the Essential Eight there are essentially two paths through it. There's a very prescriptive one with all of the checks and balances for all the controls. Where that, for various reasons, isn't possible or well suited to a particular system or service or particular type of network based on the usage or the technology within it, compensating controls can be used. What the ANAO is really referring to there is not so much around the use of compensating controls but the cadence with which we tested the efficacy of those compensating controls against the intent of each of the Essential Eight.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: What's the difference between maturity level 2 and maturity level 3? My understanding is that in 2024 the department assessed itself as meeting maturity level 2, but the ANAO's report stated that DPS self-assessed as achieving maturity level 3 for the Essential Eight in 2023-24.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Having a look at the way that the department had done its previous reporting, I think in certain circumstances and situations, it overinflated our maturity level. agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: In previous testimony or evidence that we've given at the committee, we have discussed that there have been a range of senior level departures from DPS in the ICT area. witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner

but I think the service you guys provide is brilliant.

The ANAO found instances where cybersecurity risks remained assigned to system owners who had subsequently left the department. How was that allowed to happen, and what changes have been implemented to ensure security risks are reassigned and properly managed when staff leave?

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
The first recommendation was that DPS review its governance arrangements and risk assessment process. As a result, we have established a dedicated cyber governance risk and assurance function within the Cyber Security Branch. This has been incredibly important to centralising the work that we're doing in relation to risk and assurance in relation to cyber. That team has done an incredible amount of work already in centralising the risk assessment register that we have on cyber risks. It did not used to be centralised; it was dispersed. That led to this issue that you have raised and the ANAO raised, which is that there were risk assessments dispersed through the Information Services Division, and possibly elsewhere, which were not being properly moved—or responsibilities weren't being moved—when people were moving on, and they weren't being looked at and reviewed as a whole across the system.

As a result, as I said, we've established that team. We've centralised the risk register. At the moment, they are going through a process of reviewing all of the risks that are in the centralised risk register. They've identified—and I find this quite shocking—104 historical risk assessments that were marked complete but had no assessment evidence. This is the issue that the ANAO was raising with us. They've now identified that and are in the process of reviewing those historical risk assessments. They're now also working on 33 new risk assessments. They've got 18 new cyber assessments in progress, and they've also done in that time 61 new cyber-risk assessments. So this team is absolutely running to deal with that issue that the ANAO has raised.

For the application process, we will receive an application for a sponsored access card. That undergoes the eligibility suitability test. When it does come back through to the pass office, that is then further processed, the applicants advised, payments received and appointments made, and the applicant can come in and make their new card. agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
My question is for the President. As this is my workplace, we have raised with you multiple times racism in this building and racism in the chamber. Can you tell me what's happening? What are you doing about it?

The President: I have responded to you in writing. I don't have that letter with me, but I have responded to your concerns. As I've said on multiple occasions, the standing orders cover certain behaviours, and where those behaviours are on display in the Senate, if I'm in the chair, I ask for them to be withdrawn. Where there are personal reflections against senators, which is a breach of the standing orders, if I'm in the chair, I ask for them to be withdrawn. As I've said on numerous occasions in the Senate, the way that the standing order applies is that it has to be dealt with at that time because comments by other senators and interjections are invariably not caught by the Hansard. You can't really go back and view the video evidence and come to any conclusion because, even though it sounds very loud in the Senate at the time, when you look at the video recording, it's not there, which is why those remarks which senators find are offensive do need to be dealt with in the chamber at that time. I would be much happier if senators were more respectful in their behaviour, and that goes to all of us. I say many times when I'm chairing the Senate that it is my responsibility to try and ensure that the chamber is respectful. That isn't always the case. If it isn't and I'm in the chair, I draw it to senators' attention.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
So is it okay to be racist in the chamber? Is it acceptable?

The President: Well, acceptable standards are judged by the standing orders.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
The racist speeches, the racism—turning your back on the Welcome to Country acknowledgement to country is a form of racism—so what are the rules?

The President: My responsibilities and my actions are covered by the standing orders. Where it is a breach of the standing orders, I will, if I'm in the chair, draw it to senators' attention, and many senators here I've asked to withdraw various comments at particular times. If I'm in the chair, I ask for the withdrawal to happen, but my role as president is limited to standing orders, or I will often ask a senator to reflect on how their behaviour or the comment that they've made may have upset another senator and I will ask for that senator, in the interests of the chamber, to withdraw a remark, which I've done countless times.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
The letter that you're referring to, is that the letter that you received from Senator Payman, Senator Faruqi and me?

The President: Yes.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
Can you tell me why you included One Nation in your response to us, to the three women of colour, asking you to step in and stop racism in the chamber? You then responded and included Pauline Hanson.

The President: Well, as I said to you—

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:

The President: Well, that's a conclusion you can draw.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
Well, that's what we felt—all of us.

The President: I disagree with you. I don't have of—

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
Of course you would.
