agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
You got a letter from three women of colour—senators—about the racism and you responded and put Pauline Hanson in that letter. That was a letter from the three of us. Sorry I haven't finished.

The President: Well, I'm going to respond.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Sorry, I haven't finished.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
I'm going to just ask everyone to just take turns so that everyone has a chance to have their say, so you can ask your questions and so the questions you were asked are responded to.

The President: Senator Thorpe, you chose to publish the letter in the media before I got it, so let's not be—

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
So that's why you included Pauline Hanson in a letter to the three black women that are raising an issue with you?

The President: As I said to you, Senator Thorpe, I don't have the letter in front of me. My recollection is that you made statements in relation to that senator, so, as a matter of courtesy, I included that senator in the response.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
Do you understand the harm that that caused to the three women of colour who put that letter to you? Do you understand the harm that you caused?

The President: Senator Thorpe, it is my responsibility as the President to be transparent. If I have a letter that makes statements about another senator, then it is my responsibility to make sure that the senator is also part of my response, because that senator may wish to make their own contribution.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
Can I be clear about the process then. If someone writes a letter to you—you're meant to be in control of the Senate. They write a letter to you and they say: 'We're not feeling very safe here. We're being attacked every day when we come to work in your workplace that you run.' We wrote to you saying, 'Can you please do something about it?' and you respond with the perpetrator.

The President: They're your words, Senator Thorpe. They're not mine. You wrote a letter to me which you then chose to publish in the media, so it was not a secret. It had been published in the media. I responded to that letter. If a senator is named in that letter, then I will include that senator in the response. I am not in control of the workplace. This parliament belongs to all parliamentarians.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
You're in control of the Senate.

The President: We all have a sense of responsibility to make this a safe workplace. When I am in the chamber, it is my role as the President to uphold the standing orders, which I take very seriously. I am concerned about the disrespect, generally, from many senators in the chamber to one another and to me. If you look at my record, I pull senators up when that disrespect is evident to me, either to another senator or to me.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
I just don't understand the process and the health and wellbeing aspect of responding the way you did and including the perpetrator in that event. Does that then mean, for anybody who writes to you, that you will always respond with the alleged perpetrator copied in? Is that the process?

The President: As I've said, Senator Thorpe, a senator was named in that letter. It is my responsibility in putting a response together to alert that senator to my comments. That is open and transparent.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
It's also very dangerous and very harmful. I'd like you to reconsider and make sure, for the people writing to you about the harm that they are experiencing, that you take that a little bit more seriously next time and you maybe call or email and let them know that you're including the perpetrator into the correspondence.

The President: Senator Thorpe, that's a term you're using. Your letter to me—the writers of that letter or their staff chose to publish it in the media, so it was open to anyone to make a response. It named another senator. It is beholden on me, as the President, to ensure an open and transparent response and to ensure that the senator named was aware of what I had said as the President.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
I understand what you're saying. I'm just asking you if you could consider the harm caused.

The President: They're your words, Senator Thorpe. They're not mine.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
Can anyone else from a DPS perspective—

The President: This is the Department of Parliamentary Services. It's not the Senate.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text: Senator, this is not an issue that relates to DPS.
witness_organisation: Department of Parliamentary Services

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
No. No-one really wants to deal with racism in this place. It is a very unsafe workplace, and—I'm sorry—you don't make it any easier.

The President: If I can add to that, I've just now looked at the letter, and I would like to put on the record that Senator Hanson was not copied in as a response.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner
text:
Okay, so just to be clear, the letter was published by those who sent it to you.

The President: Yes, that's correct. And in my response, I responded to the three senators who were authors to that letter. Whilst there was a reference to another senator, that senator was absolutely not copied into the letter. So Senator Thorpe's line of questioning is not correct—or her assertion that I copied another senator into the response, who was not an author to that letter, is not correct.

agency: Department of Parliamentary Services Parliamentary Service Commissioner

Yes.

If you can give an update on where we are with the completion dates, what the original budget was and where we are with expenditure and expected completion dates and so forth.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'd like to welcome the honourable Minister McCarthy, and Ms Julie-Ann Guivarra and other officers of the National Indigenous Australians Agency. Minister, would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
I'd like to acknowledge that we come together on the lands of the Ngunnawal and Ngambri peoples and pay my respects to elders past, present and emerging. I'd like to put my words on the record about Dr Haines. We are certainly deeply saddened and troubled by what we've seen occur recently. We are sending our love and best wishes to her and her family, as well as recognising the work that she's done and will continue to do when she comes out. We hope she will continue to work with First Nations people and families to improve the lives of our people across the country. She's been a very committed person to closing the gap with our committees and has tried to assist, and in her numerous correspondences and discussions with me over the years.

I'd also like to put on the record just what has happened to us as a parliament. I'm very conscious that we deal with family and domestic violence right across this country, especially with First Nations families. With all people who are experiencing any kind of hurt, it does have an ability to see something like this bring back trauma of all sorts. I want to put on the record here that the behaviour in the parliament, particularly in the Senate, needs to be looked into even more. I, too, have concerns when I see senators turning their back on the acknowledgement of country every morning, and I put my voice on the record in support of Senator Thorpe with what's going on with Senator Hanson about the satirical cartoons—supposedly funny. I've learnt of that today, and I find it absolutely reprehensible that that continues, and I would certainly ask for consideration to be given to what's going on there, too. I want to say to Senator Thorpe that I don't agree with that, and I find it absolutely reprehensible.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you, Minister McCarthy. I think those in the room would echo your sentiments. We'll start with Senator Liddle, and we'll go in 10-minute blocks.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
I start with a question about prominent Voice campaigners and Indigenous leaders Thomas Mayo, Pat Anderson and Travis Lovett, who've all criticised the government's lack of policy direction in Indigenous affairs. On the third anniversary of the Voice, Ken Wyatt said:

What statements have you seen from the Minister for Indigenous Affairs that are proactive since the Voice? And what has come from the Prime Minister? He was very active during the Voice. Since the Voice, there's been very little.

I ask: does the Albanese government have a single, overarching policy for the Indigenous Australians portfolio, and, if so, what is it?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We are working on closing the gap, the national agreement and the coordination of that across the country. One of the things that I said quite often throughout the Voice campaign, when I was asked, 'What will you do if people vote no?' was: 'It means that people want the status quo.' Here, in the parliament, we have, as part of that, the National Agreement on Closing the Gap. What I've been doing is picking up the strength of that to try and look at all those targets and see what we can do to ensure that parliaments all across the country commit to their commitment to that agreement. People may not like that, but that's what we're doing.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: So close the gap is not a policy; it's an objective. Is that right?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It's certainly our objective, but it is a policy as far as the agencies and departments are concerned. We have a ministerial working group on Closing the Gap in terms of working directly with the ministers of each of the state and territory governments, and that is a clear direction that we are going in. That is the one that we are focused on. It doesn't mean we can't focus on other matters. We certainly are doing that as well, but this is our clear focus at the moment.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Minister, three years on from the failure of the Voice referendum, does your government remain committed to treaty and truth?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I have always maintained that the principles of the Uluru Statement from the Heart are still with us.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Minister, it was very disappointing that the NIAA annual report was tabled for a review by parliamentarians on Friday afternoon last week. It doesn't leave a bit of time for people to do analysis, but anyway. Here we are. NIAA, when did you provide that to the minister?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: The annual report was provided to the minister on 15 October.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: On 15 October—just in time for Senate estimates.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: My error—I did not give Ms Guivarra a chance for an opening statement. My sincere apologies. Would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you, Chair. It's not a formal statement. I did want to acknowledge, in fact, that our annual report had been tabled. The second issue was to introduce Josh Smith, who is our new Deputy CEO of Policies and Programs. He's not so new now. He's been with us for a few months. He has taken over the policy and program role that I was previously in. That was it.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: My apologies, Senator, for interrupting your line of questioning.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: That's okay. Continuing on the theme that we often hear in this place, which is listening to people out there in communities, one thing I noticed was that the level of complaints about NIAA in 2024-25 was 192 and in 2025-26 that's 275. That's a 43 per cent increase in complaints to NIAA about, one would assume, people's service and people's engagement with NIAA. Can you explain that?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'll hand across to Sean Worth, who's in charge of our integrity team, soon. But the one thing I would say in regard to our formal complaints mechanism is that we do in fact have a formal complaints mechanism and we certainly encourage both community and providers to submit complaints to that. In terms of seeing a number of complaints increase, we wouldn't necessarily see that as a bad thing. It's important that we actually provide the opportunity, as I said, for both providers and for community to come forward with issues that they feel need to be addressed. We've done similar work recently with our indigenous advancement strategy, which of course is our main funding. You'll be aware that we've recently opened up a survey for all providers and all community, in fact, to come forward with ways in which they could see us improving the Indigenous Advancement Strategy. I'll turn to Mr Worth to see if he has anything further to add in relation to the numbers.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I've got the numbers, Mr Worth. We're really pressed for time, so I'm going to go straight to it. What is the nature of the complaints? People are clearly unhappy if you've got an increase of 43 per cent.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We receive complaints across a whole range of different matters. Approximately one-third of the complaints that we receive are actually not complaints for the NIAA themselves. Whilst they're included within that total because those are the total received, they're not in relation to the operations of the NIAA, so they are referred to other agencies where relevant.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: So what you're saying is that this is a 43 per cent increase in complaints to the body that is known to manage Indigenous Australians about what is happening for people in Indigenous affairs right across the government.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
Yes. Approximately 50 per cent of the complaints that we receive do relate to some element of the service that we might be funding—provider related complaints. Those are then referred within the agency to the appropriate regional areas so that they can work through the nature of those. The other complaint categories are spread across a number of different areas of First Nations interests and native title concerns that people might have regarding their own claims and how long it's taking to go through whatever process it is, as well as a number of others.

There has been an increase in the number. We have been investing a lot of effort within the agency to ensure that we can receive and respond to those complaints as appropriate. It is something that we have been investing in to increase the trust, so, for those people who do make complaints, they can have a level of confidence that these complaints will actually be dealt with. It would naturally be concerning—if we didn't deal with complaints, people would give up on the process.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It was something that we discussed at our executive board just last week, and one of the other trends that we are noticing is the proliferation of complaints generated by AI. It was a conversation that we had around—and this is not an uncommon issue across other Public Service agencies as well—responding in a timely manner to what is an increase in the number of complaints across complaint mechanisms, in other agencies as well, largely generated by artificial intelligence.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Can you tell me how many of those actually are. It's pretty obvious if they're form letters, if they're AI generated. It's a big claim to say that AI is playing a part in this.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: By no means are all complaints AI generated, but there are some clear markers for those that are clearly AI generated. Instead of being perhaps a one- or two-page letter of complaint, we could be receiving up to 15 or 16 pages of AI generated text that often brings in matters quite unrelated to the nature of the complaint itself. It is resulting in additional effort and time from the complaints team to analyse these letters and understand the nature of the complaint, understand who the appropriate party is that we can deal with so that we can, as I said before, ensure that we are dealing with complaints as quickly as we can and as appropriately as we can.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
It's interesting because complaints to my office have actually gone up as well. I can tell there's somebody on the end of the phone when I respond to those phone calls and letters.

I want to go to a question you were asked by Senator Nampijinpa Price in budget estimates in May about the spend in Indigenous affairs. You took a question on notice, and that was question NIAA 0012, but you didn't actually provide a complete spend in the answer. Do you know the complete spend across all portfolios? Do you have a figure?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: NIAA doesn't have the capacity to seek from the entire Commonwealth the measurement of spend on Indigenous Australians. We always strive to give you the best information that we can of the information that we can control. The last time one of those types of exercises was undertaken was the Productivity Commission report several years ago now.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I find it extraordinary that we can't get a number on what that spend is when we're talking about several departments that are delivering programs that we can identify are for improving the lives of Indigenous peoples, their communities and their organisations. Do we know who's spending it? Do we know what they're spending it on? How can we find that out in a collective? If we did some mapping—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I think that it's probably a question that you might need to take up with central agencies like Department of Finance or Department of Treasury. There are obviously a range of departments across the Commonwealth that are funding a funding Indigenous programs in a very targeted way, but there are obviously then also the broader programs which touch on First Nations people as well, like the welfare payments and such that cover the entire population of the country as well, including First Nations people.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I might be able to add a little bit to Mr Creagh's answer. Each year we also publish a First Nations budget fact sheet, which provides visibility of all the First Nations expenditure across all portfolios. For example, the 2026-27 budget fact sheet, which is available on the NIAA website, outlined a number of measures totalling $1.2 billion to be invested over five years. Other departments also release fact sheets outlining portfolio-specific measures. In addition to that, you're asking how you could map it. You can get the details of those measures in their Portfolio Budget Statements as well. Mr Creagh was right around the last review from the Productivity Commission, which provided a more comprehensive look at Indigenous expenditure. I think that was around 2017. The next Productivity Commission review of the National Agreement on Closing the Gap has just commenced, and there is one line item in their terms of reference which goes to looking at expenditure on the national agreement, which might provide a bit more detail as well, once that concludes.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you very much. We'll go to Senator Thorpe.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you for appearing today. My first question is about Mount Isa. This is to the minister, Minister McCarthy. When did you and your office become aware of issues with the housing provider that was responsible for managing Aboriginal housing in Mount Isa?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you. I know we've provided information to you in the Senate in terms of your OPD. I believe I responded, to your question on this in the Senate, that I first became aware of it in April.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: April this year?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'll have to get the dates. Yes.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you. According to your department's understanding of the CATSI Act, what steps were available to you and NIAA to prevent the loss of these homes that were under the corporation's management and so many people, including elders, losing their homes?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We went through quite a lot of steps and many processes in terms of, firstly, what we could do with the corporation. I'll go to the NIAA in a moment, but I do want to put on the record there was considerable work done between the NIAA office in Mount Isa with staff here. Certainly, I went to Mount Isa to meet with families, trying to look at working with the Mount Isa council—they were perhaps my first port of call—to really see if this debt could be waived, for starters. Just what was it that they wanted? I reached out to the Queensland government for their assistance as well, given there was a legacy issue around the houses in terms of former agreements with the state and, of course, through ORIC itself to see if we could look at other options in terms of trying to assist these families. But I'll hand over to NIAA in terms of some of the more technical aspects of it.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you. As the minister said, we became aware of the situation with the houses in Mount Isa when it was actually the Mount Isa council that reached out to us seeking the withdrawal of caveats which were over the properties. Those caveats existed back from when the organisation in question was actually under ATSIC, and we actually did look at that issue around whether those caveats would apply in a circumstance where a local council was actually seeking to basically reclaim rates through the sale of those properties. We found, through the legal advice, that in fact the Queensland government and local government acts in Queensland actually gazumped any rights we had to prevent those sales from happening through the caveat itself. As the minister has also noted, we did go through a range of different consultations with the Mount Isa City Council, at every level. I had meetings with the mayor and councillors. The minister did as well. Our office in Mount Isa has done similarly throughout this process. We also reached out to the Department of Housing and Public Works in Queensland, who are actually responsible for social housing in Queensland.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: The houses are gone. The property developer just sailed in, bought up 12 of them and made our people homeless. Would you do things differently? When you find out that our people in Aboriginal housing need a million bucks to bail them out—it ended up only being $600,000 or $700,000 in the end—that money could have saved 15 families to stay in Aboriginal housing. Would you do the same thing if it came around again? Where do you step in and say, 'No, we need as much housing as we possibly can get; we're going to find 600 grand to pay these rates'? How do we not make that same mistake? Where are those elders? Where are those families? Are they all housed?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'll actually let the group manager responsible for eastern talk about the circumstances a little bit in relation to the tenants, but you can appreciate—and there will be an opportunity, obviously, to speak to ORIC tomorrow as well—that there were some complications, obviously, associated with the organisation itself. I think, publicly, ORIC has been clear that there was an investigation that was undertaken.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Yes.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: From about July, we became aware of it. In addition to that, of course, through this process, ORIC has put in place a special administrator and now a liquidator. Our priority throughout—and I think we discussed this when we briefed you as well, some time back—was looking at what could be done to support the tenants. As I said, we went through a range of different activities directly with the tenants, where we organised pop-up meetings and sessions with the tenants and also service providers in the community to see if there were alternatives that could be provided, as well as the Queensland government, who have, as I understand it, now assisted several of those families. A complication with the tenants, as well, was that not all of those families were in fact eligible for social housing given the income levels of the families, but I will just defer to our group managers to go through a little bit more in terms of what's happening with the tenants now, because that was part of your question.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thanks. The community actually had a self-determining model that they wanted to put in place, but that was also denied by NIAA. The alternative was for the community to determine for themselves and establish their own provider, but that wasn't afforded to the community.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: As I said, there are, in part, complications associated with the situation of the organisation itself.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: The previous organisation.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It still has been in existence, until such time as ORIC has now put in a special administrator and a liquidator. There were definitely issues associated with the ability to deal with the directors of the organisation at the time, which, in terms of others then stepping in to exercise self-determination as an alternative—those were things that we had looked at. We also met with Queensland Housing and the Aboriginal community controlled housing peak and others to look at whether there were options on that, but I'll turn to Ms Pattrick.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
I will go to the tenants, but, just to add to what our CEO was saying, the ownership of the property rested with the organisation, so we weren't able to enact the caveats, as the CEO has said, which would prevent the sale. Essentially a newly established body would still have needed to work with the existing body that was not operational to be able to enact a sale to the new organisation. The difficulty was that because there was no operational board there was no-one for a new organisation to engage with, and we couldn't stop the sale through the council, because their legislation overrode ours.

In regard to the tenants, we acknowledge that tenants are still working through their arrangements, but we have been advised that a number of tenants—I want to say fewer than five, because I don't want to give away personal information—have found alternative accommodation and are in the process of moving. We also understand that there are another three tenants who are working through getting properties at the moment.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Senator Thorpe, if you're going to change topic, I'm going to rotate the call—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Go for it.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: and then we'll come back.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Yes. Totally.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Senator Pocock.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you. I want to pursue a housing matter also. Minister, I want to ask about the recent closure of the YiSSA facility in Darwin. You've said that the Commonwealth government offered to cover the full cost of transferring ownership of the facility to local ACCO Yilli Rreung, but the Northern Territory government refused that. Did you meet with the minister and the chief minister about the Commonwealth's offer? And when did you do that, if you did?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
I'm certainly happy to provide a time line. I think I'll just speak more broadly now, if I can, and then give you the actual dates and figures post now. When the minister made the announcement in July that it was going to close in October, the reasons provided by the Northern Territory minister came down to costs and that they didn't want to renew the lease from Ausco, who owned the demountables and were leasing the property in terms of the land—it's Crown land. So their lease on the land was coming up in October. For whatever reasons between the Northern Territory government and Ausco, there was no agreement met, so the minister made the announcement to close it down and move everyone out, which is when I reached out to the Northern Territory government to ask, 'Can we have a look at what's going on here?' We're talking about a 400-bed facility, and it's been incredibly important to have that facility for those hundreds of families over the years, especially more recently with the wet season earlier this year, when so many more were displaced.

We engaged over probably a month or so to try to look at what was possible. In that time I made the offer. Obviously we reached out to Ausco as well, because I felt that the breakdown had been between Ausco and the Northern Territory government, so I wanted to understand from Ausco what the issue was. My understanding was that Ausco wanted $6.5 million for the next 90 days that the offer would be on the table to actually purchase the demountables, and after that the figure would increase.

So we virtually had 90 days to try to reach some kind of agreement, and that was where we looked at the offer of $6.5 million, provided that an Aboriginal organisation ran the facility, and that organisation is Yilli Rreung. They have been running it for a number of years and have been very capable to do so, and we wanted to see the ownership belong to them. But we would still need to lease the land from the Northern Territory government, given that it's Crown land. That offer was not accepted. Realising that they wanted to own the assets, or at least have some stake in it, we lowered the offer to $3.5 million on top of their $3 million, which they already had—still with the proviso that Yilli Rreung would be at the table to run the facility.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: So the closure has proceeded?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It's happened.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Was it a breach of obligations under the Closing the Gap agreement?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: This is the conundrum with Closing the Gap. It is an agreement, but it's not—we've discussed this before in terms of financial arrangements. There are no penalties surrounding whether parliaments can be penalised for not doing the right thing according to the agreement. So the simple answer is they certainly went against the values of what the Closing the Gap agreement is all about, yes.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Can you now withhold funding under the Commonwealth agreement to reflect the money that was offered but rejected by the Northern Territory government?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: For this particular—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Yes.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
What we've done, Senator Pocock, is—I have been working with the ministerial working group on Closing the Gap, which includes the finance minister. I have said—at the beginning of this year—that I've had concerns about the fact that state and territory parliaments are not adhering to Closing the Gap, and the best way to try and enforce it is through the financial arrangements, so I have made adjustments to the Northern Territory remote area investment as a result of it. That's the first federal funding agreement which—I've incorporated changes in that through NIAA's negotiations.

The second thing I've done has been to ask the finance minister to come to the Northern Territory—which she did. We were meant to meet with the Chief Minister, but the Chief Minister took leave, so we met with the Deputy Chief Minister and put on the table our concerns, from the federal government, across a large area of funding—not just YiSSA, with housing, but also with many other areas—and, in that meeting, expressed very clearly the financial concerns and the funding arrangements that were troubling the Commonwealth and also that we would start to seriously look at other avenues of funding, particularly direct funding, to Aboriginal organisations and/or local governments.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you. I'm not sure how much time I've got, but I'd like to ask about black cladding and what due diligence is being undertaken for certificates of Aboriginality. There are a number of stat decs being used by non-Aboriginal people saying that they're Aboriginal. They're cashing in—not that we get much. But they are cashing in on the procurement process that's meant to provide economic opportunity for Aboriginal people in this country. It's cashing in on Aboriginal identified positions and accessing grants. Basically, you can get a certificate of Aboriginality from a mate on a board that will give you one. This is a big problem. What due diligence is done to ensure whitefellas aren't cashing in on the little crumbs that we get?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
We can certainly speak to some of the efforts that have been made more recently in terms of looking at reforms to the Indigenous Procurement Policy to address issues around black cladding. There have been. obviously, efforts to strengthen the thresholds for the Indigenous Procurement Policy, which was previously 50 per cent owned—now 51 per cent owned and controlled. And that will be part of, obviously, what's administered as part of the reforms.

In addition to that there is, obviously, the three-part test, which all government departments are required to look at, in terms of how they administer their programs. How they do that individually is a matter for each individual agency when they're looking at the administration of their own policies and programs. But I will get Mr Dexter just to go through in a bit more detail, because, as I said, we're looking at what we're responsible for most directly. And there are several things in addition to what I just said, in terms of the strengthening of the thresholds. There are other things that we're also doing and looking at—black cladding, specifically—as part of the reform process.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
Black cladding is a complex issue, and there are various perspectives on what is and is not black cladding and the best ways to address it and prevent it. The National Indigenous Australians Agency considers black cladding to include disempowering or disingenuous business practices, corporate arrangements or business structures that are intended to misrepresent a business as an Indigenous business when in fact it is not. One of the main things that the government is doing to address black cladding is the strengthening of the criteria around the Indigenous Procurement Policy. The move from 50 to 51 per cent might sound like a small shift, but I do want to emphasise that moving to 51 per cent, both owned and controlled, makes sure that First Nations business owners who are able to access the IPP going forward are actually empowered to run their own business and to make decisions about how that business is operating in a way that the previous definition didn't require. It didn't require that to be a part of the test.

The NIAA is also engaging with the First Nations Economic Partnership, which has listed as one of its immediate actions the strengthening of the IPP. We presented to that partnership, at the last meeting in September, on what we were doing around IPP strengthening, and they've asked us to come back to do some more work with them around black cladding as well. The government is working in partnership with our partners, the First Nations Economic Empowerment Alliance, as well as with the Coalition of Peaks, about how government can take more action to address black cladding.

I would also point to the fact that the NIAA is working with different regulators across the Commonwealth. There are different regulators with different roles they can play in this space. Certainly, our current verification services provider, which is Supply Nation, can look at whether or not a business is meeting the definition or not. That is their role to do. But there are other regulators in this space, such as ASIC, who can look at breaches of the Corporations Law; the ACCC, who can look at misleading and deceptive conduct in terms of the trade practices law; as well as, of course, law enforcement agencies, who can look at instances of fraud. So if someone has said that they are an Aboriginal person when, in fact, they are not, that, in some circumstances, might amount to fraud, which is something that law enforcement agencies can look into.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I have some questions around stolen wages. An investigation by the ABC, published on 2 September this year, raised concerns about the processes of a historical stolen wages class action in the Northern Territory—this time specifically in north-east Arnhem Land. The report raised issues about both the registration process undertaken by Shine Lawyers and Deloitte's administration of the Commonwealth settlement in the Northern Territory case. Local organisations like Aboriginal Resource and Development Services have needed to respond to information and frustration from local mob. Much of this work has been unfunded, despite this community involvement being ordered by the Federal Court and both Shine and Deloitte receiving millions from the settlement. Minister, while it seems you cannot comment on the specifics of the Federal Court orders or Deloitte's administration, is the government satisfied with how the settlement of this matter has been handled?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency

I've certainly had families raise questions with me earlier on in the piece around being able to access stolen wages and wondering how they can do that. It is clearly in Shine Lawyers' purview to have that direct responsibility, but I am very aware that there have been concerns raised.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: In the future, will you review this method of administration?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency

I think it's important to be able to have a look at that process and see what could have been done differently.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'm sure the agency has had contact with them.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Yes, Senator. I'll hand across to our general counsel. I would just say that some of the issues that you are pointing out are, obviously, a part of the Federal Court settlement, so our ability to change or influence that is actually very limited by the Federal Court's remit and its responsibilities. But, because we're involved in the settlement, we do have our general counsel who has interactions with the actual law firm. So I'll hand across to Mr Bartholomew.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'm really trying to focus not on a big, long account about what's happened—I don't want to be rude—but what are the lessons here, and what do we need to be doing differently?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: The court appointed administrators do regularly report. Those reports are public and under the supervision of Chief Justice Mortimer, who's the presiding judge for this matter. The most recent report was released last week, on 19 October, and I'm able to provide the secretariat with the website address if that's helpful to you, Senator. Whilst the Commonwealth can't unilaterally take any action, noting that it was a claim against the Commonwealth in the first place, there are two important steps to bring to your attention, Senator. The first step is the supervision of the court itself, and the court takes that role very seriously in terms of its supervision of the appointed administrators and the review of those reports that I've mentioned. The second step is—as you've highlighted, we are in contact with Deloitte as administrators. There was a meeting earlier this year, in April, that involved both the parties and the administrator, as well as some community organisations, that was focused on this particular community concern. The intent at the moment is for the parties to reconvene again, given the ongoing concerns that are being expressed, and if a path forward can be identified it will be for each of those parties to consider the next steps individually and then under the court's supervision of course.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Minister, the issues raised in the ABC article have led to a call for the Commonwealth to set up a national redress scheme established in partnership with Aboriginal organisations which would stay open for a period of years and provide a uniform, harmonised and more just approach—probably a whole lot less expensive too. Will the government consider such a Commonwealth redress scheme?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We're certainly watching what's happening in terms of everything that's occurred so far. I'd like to be able to take that question on notice and get back to you.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: There are very, very variable outcomes between jurisdictions, which raises a whole lot of questions about justice. I want to move then to First Nations leaders in the public sector and Public Service roles. Over the past year, we've seen a lot of prominent First Nations leaders resign from government positions out of frustration or lack of progress. Dr Eddie Cubillo quit the Commonwealth Justice Policy Partnership over failures to act on bail laws. Numerous children's commissioners have resigned over responses to child protection and incarceration. In Queensland, Joshua Creamer accused the government of implementing an organised strategy to get rid of Indigenous roles in government agencies. Is your agency monitoring the number of First Nations public servants and advisory body members resigning from positions, and how are you tracking or not tracking this really important change and loss?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
Certainly, we're looking at it at the Commonwealth level. Again, we have had—and I think we've spoken about them previously at Senate estimates—initiatives in the Commonwealth Public Service to increase the number of First Nations senior executive service. There was an initiative called the SES100, which we ran with the Australian Public Service Commission. We're keeping active monitoring of what's happening with the numbers under the SES100, and I'll get our COO, Ms Jackson, to talk about that briefly.

In relation to what's happening in other jurisdictions, we are aware of some of those resignations that you have referred to. There's a number that have happened in the Northern Territory. In Queensland, we know that there's been a number of appointments of First Nations people that haven't been renewed by the Queensland government in recent times. Yes, in general terms, we are keeping track of what's happening across those jurisdictions. Again, though, to the minister's point earlier, she looks at all of these issues in relation to what's happening on closing the gap. One of those issues, obviously, is what's happening in transformation under priority reform 3 of government in the ways it's dealing with First Nations communities. Part of that is actually the responsibility of those jurisdictions—states and territories—to be looking at how they're addressing systemic racism in their own services.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'm sure I can find out about the program. Do you review APSC reports and staff surveys with a particular lens on racism within the public service?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We recently provided evidence to the joint standing committee on racism, and it brought to our attention a lot of the employee experiences in the APS, which I spoke about at that inquiry. We work very closely with the Australian Public Service Commission, who do that monitoring and produce reports and share reports based on different cohorts of people, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander staff, in the APS who report experiences of racism in the Public Service. We support the Indigenous champions network in looking at racism as a particular priority. Secretary Jones is the chair of the Indigenous champions network. We work closely with the Indigenous SES network and the Indigenous cross-agency network to hear from their experiences as well. We are in the process of developing a priority reform strategy following the release of the recent Commonwealth priority reforms roadmap, which is a Commonwealth initiative. A particular pillar of that is eliminating racism in the Public Service.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Have you spoken with Dr Cubillo; the former commissioner, Mr Creamer, or others about what led to their resignations?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I think Dr Cubillo actually issued a letter at the time of his resignation from the Justice Policy Partnership as to the reasons why he chose not to continue to participate with the JPP. We have, from time to time, had interactions with Dr Creamer about what was happening, obviously, around the time of the truth-telling inquiries and their cessation in Queensland. We are aware of the issues. Some of it has actually, to the point that Rachael has also raised, come up in the context of the racism inquiry that the government and the minister had called for earlier this year. I think there's 700-odd submissions to that inquiry that have indicated that there is an experience of racism, and that's not just First Nations people in communities, it is also an experience of public servants as well. I would say it exists, and it's a thing that we have to deal with.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: What do you specifically do to encourage and support First Nations people into leadership?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
Within the Public Service, we do have the SES 100 initiative, and we are working with the Public Service Commission to run more programs under that initiative shortly. That includes not only recruiting to senior executive positions but there are also development pathways, a senior executive service program called Yawarra, and an executive-level program called Bulabul that supports that career pipeline to senior executive roles. We, through the CEO—her role on the Secretaries Board—regularly talk about First Nations representation at senior leadership tables and promote not only recruitment but development, for First Nations staff, into those senior leadership roles. That's not just the recruitment element; it's the conversation around cultural safety in those environments, particularly where there are not, in some departments, very many senior leaders in those roles.

There's a big conversation about cultural safety at the moment in the COO Collaboration Circle, which is a formal mechanism under the Chief Operating Officers Committee, in the Public Service, that has a number of chief operating officers meet with First Nations staff from across the Public Service at different levels but in a way that brings people together where there's no hierarchy. One of the issues that we're talking about at the moment is cultural safety. We've been working with Comcare on further definitions and information for departments about their response and promotion of cultural safety in the workplace. There are a bunch of other programs I could talk about, but I imagine you're short on time.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We'll go to Senator Liddle.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I want to follow up on the remote jobs. You said remote jobs was funded for $965 million and was not ongoing—that it was not going to go up—and then you told me it was funded on an ongoing basis. How much per annum is being spent on RJP, and is that indexed? If you can't provide it now, you can certainly provide it on notice.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'll just get the specific figure in front of me. I believe, to 30 June this year, it was $132 million. Yes, $132 million had been spent of that administered funding—had been paid out the door—for those existing projects that were approved last year. We approved around 300 projects last year, for 1,700 jobs, and $132 million so far has been paid of that administered funding.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency
witness_position: Branch Manager, Remote Jobs and Employment Programs Branch

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'm going to ask a question now on the child protection crisis in Port Hedland—and we know it's a problem everywhere. We've seen six weeks of horrific reporting out of Port Hedland, but it was only after a delegation of state and federal coalition MPs that made a trip—Minister, you showed up after that. Why did it take you so long, and when did you first plan that trip?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We set up the children's commissioner as a national position for First Nations children right across the country. That position came into effect officially, through the legislation, in July. It was important to enable that space for the children's commissioner to actually go to Port Hedland, to have time with the families, to also get to Perth and hold her roundtable. When she came back, I then received a briefing and made the decision to go, after the briefing from our commissioner.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It was still some five weeks after it had first been reported extensively, though, that the commissioner went over there.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I think what's important here, Senator Liddle, is that the commissioner went to Port Hedland, and what's important is that there is currently a real focus through the work that she's doing—and, certainly, in the work that we're all trying to do—to improve the lives of children.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: When did you become aware that the Western Australian government was refusing a call for a coronial inquest?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I think, like most people, you read the Australian. The Australian—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It was six weeks.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: has certainly had consistent coverage, daily, on what was happening in Western Australia. It was very clear through that. Post my visit and perhaps before—I'd have to have a look at the order. But I'd certainly reached out to the WA government—I think it was on the last day of sittings here—in terms of a briefing directly with the child protection minister responsible, to be able to get that briefing from her.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'm going to turn to extensive reporting—still in Western Australia—about Julyardi director Raylene Button organising a fight club, with children present, and, in another native title corporation, throwing a fellow director to the floor. They were images that were portrayed in news stories. There were also reports about extensive integrity issues around representation of local people: five members on the board, recirculating for many years. It's an organisation that receives $13 million in Commonwealth funding. When did you first become aware of these issues and what steps did you take to assure yourself that that is a fit organisation to receive Commonwealth funding?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: As we do, with organisations or individuals that are identified in the media, the relevant agency or department will write directly to that organisation to ask for a 'please explain'. I'll just refer now to the CEO.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: There were a number of agency heads, because, in fact, there are several Commonwealth agencies that are funders of Julyardi, not just NIAA; the Department of Social Services and the Department of Education have also provided funding over the period. So, when we became aware of the initial incident, we, as secretaries, wrote to the board and the chair of Julyardi seeking explanations of what had occurred. When the second video was released, we also followed up with other organisations which we fund that have the particular person in question as a director of those organisations. So we've actually reached out now to all of the relevant organisations. I'll just turn to Ms Smith and see if there's anything further to add at this stage.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: No, nothing further to add.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: The Central Australian Aboriginal Congress, back in July, put out a media release saying that—and I applaud them, because I have raised this many times—no-one on their board can now have a criminal record and serve on their boards. Why, Minister, haven't you, with the stroke of a pen, made that—have you started that work?—a requirement for any Commonwealth funding for all organisations that receive funding, given the issues we have with family and domestic violence? Have you started that work?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We've certainly engaged with ORIC on that, because most of these organisations do come under the Corporations Act, and it is important to see what's possible. I'm looking at, certainly, a review of the CATSI Act to look at that. But I will refer now to the CEO. These are important questions, and we are working on it.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: There are several things that we would check, in terms of integrity, in relation to organisations that we do fund. There are requirements in head agreements around the conduct and fit-and-proper-person requirements in our funding agreements. So those things are routinely checked through our compliance processes. But I will just check with Mr Worth whether there's anything else on that particular aspect.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: No. I'd confirm that, at this stage, we have got, as mentioned by Ms Guivarra, the fit-and-proper-person test, particularly focused on individuals involved in the management or in service delivery directly—where the key risks lie, as you can appreciate.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Clearly there are plenty of gaps. On the murder of Kumanjayi Little Baby: at last estimates it was revealed that Tangentyere Council receives almost $82 million in Commonwealth funding. What steps have you taken to assure yourself and the Australian people that Commonwealth funding in Alice Springs town camps remains appropriate and fit for purpose? What changes have been made to NIAA's grant monitoring and reporting arrangements since that tragic event?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I will hand to Ms Bellenger.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text:
Certainly we responded to the question on notice with all of the KPIs and reports from the last estimates. Tangentyere are still fully compliant in the services that they are delivering. The way that we monitor progress and what's actually happening is through site visits—actually attending in the town camps and some of the activities that are run. So we are talking not only to Tangentyere as the service organisation but also to community members that access that service.

I would also go on to say—in terms of the second part to your question, about what we have done—that we provided immediate support to the family, as you're likely aware, after the incident, and that support continued until it was no longer necessary. We also have put a partnership together with Tangentyere, the Northern Territory government Department of Housing, Local Government and Community Development and ourselves, and we're working through a list of town camp president priorities around community safety. For example, under old arrangements, where there was an incident that involved a locked door or a broken window, Tangentyere, through the housing arrangements, had to report to the NT government to get permission to get that fixed. So we've been closely working with partners, and there has been an agreed change of process now where they can go. If it's related to safety for residents, they are able to do that and do repairs and maintenance immediately.

We continue to work with the town camp presidents. They're bringing a number of different actions forward to us. They are still deliberating on some of those, but certainly I expect you'll see some funding announcements in the near future.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We will go to Senator Thorpe.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I won't be long. I just want to clarify the NTRAI agreement. Just to be clear, was the Commonwealth originally planning to provide the full $842 million to the NT government to administer? It's now being cut from the NT government, and approximately $119 million has been redistributed to be provided as grants to Aboriginal organisations. So was it originally planning to give the whole amount to the NT government?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: In the previous agreement, that would have happened with the whole amount, other than a small component to the non-government schools organisation. It was very deliberate in the drafting of this new agreement that we would do that differently. I think, as we've said, that the Aboriginal peak's involved, and there is also the sector strengthening. So that was the learning and reform from the last agreement to this new agreement, and it was deliberate.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Okay. So it's not a cut to the NTRAI agreement, and it will represent a $119 million uplift to grants made available to our organisations and communities?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Not quite. My apologies if I have not been clear in that. What I would say is that some of that money is for APO NT as the organisation to actually build their participation and capacity at the table. Seventy million of that will be grants to the ACCO sector for sector strengthening and so on, and some of that investment goes directly to the non-government organisations for the schools and homelands and remote communities as well. I can provide, on notice, a breakdown of those to be really clear.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: That'd be great.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: There will potentially be some change to schedules coming forward, though.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Was this cut—sorry, this decision—because the Northern Territory government's really racist and really bad and it's not supporting our people one bit? Is this a result of the NT government not doing the right thing?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I would say it was a deliberate reform. Our funding profile has changed over time for the NIAA to have more money. If you look at our IAS grants, the majority of money goes straight to the ground, predominantly to ACCOs. I think we're working through our arrangements at the federal level to get the best outcomes we can.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: With this other money, will that differ from the money available through IAS grants?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: No, it doesn't; it actually strengthens people's capacity to engage in that.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Are you asking whether funding out of the FFA is in addition to what's delivered through the Indigenous Advancement Strategy?
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Yes—is it a different process?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It's a different bucket. I just wanted to make sure. The Indigenous Advancement Strategy is as Ms Bellenger said. We have a focus on community controlled and First Nations organisations. More than 80 per cent—86 per cent in value terms—of our funding now goes through First Nations organisations in that process. NTRAI came off shortly off the back of what we did in the Northern Territory housing agreement, and both of those had an overarching partnership agreement over the top of them which had Commonwealth, Northern Territory government and peak organisations. In the case of housing, it was the land councils. It's the same council that was followed for NTRAI. Essentially, we are trying every chance we get these days with the FFAs that we are responsible for to try to do them in partnership with community controlled organisations.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Can we take more money off the Northern Territory government? They're committing genocide against our people in the Northern Territory. There's no doubt. The evidence is there that they are committing genocide today, in 2026, against Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory. They have no intention of doing the right thing by our people, so how much more can we take off them and give directly to the people?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: The difference in the agreements that we do have is that they have the community controlled organisations at the table. Those questions around whether funding is at the appropriate level et cetera will be things that are discussed with community controlled organisations at the table. As Ms Bellenger said, all payments are made in arrears as they do the due diligence checks. Once we get the payment request from the Northern Territory government, it still has to go through checks within the agency. It then goes to the joint steering committees for the agreement, and then it goes to a delegate. There is an opportunity for community to have a say in whether they think the things that the Northern Territory government is claiming at the time is fair and reasonable representation of what they've actually expended.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I would confirm that both of the two large agreements that NIAA hold with the Northern Territory government require a partnership approach. That is the funding that we now provide to the Northern Territory government—it's all done in partnership.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Unfortunately, the other partner's not doing the right thing, so the other partner needs to be cut. Can we cut them out altogether and have the NTRAI given to the people? Can we continue to do that?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: One of the things that is being looked at is the strength of the community control sector. That $79 million that was referred to earlier is to make sure that community are able to take on more services over time. That's part of the effort.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We just wouldn't want to see them not be capable and fall down. That's really what I'm watching here.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Will you look at the remote housing agreement as well, given we know there are big problems with negotiating that agreement? We know that Leeanne Caton has spoken about this and has quit in protest over the Northern Territory government; is that something that would be looked at as well?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We've had discussions with Ms Caton before she left the position. It was built into the partnership agreement, but there's a two-year review of the Northern Territory housing agreement currently under way, and part of that effort will be to see if there are ways of improving delivery. There have been some issues between the Commonwealth and the Northern Territory government about what is incorporated into that agreement.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Senator O'Sullivan?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I wanted to ask in relation to Port Hedland. Senator McCarthy, you may know I've been up there twice in the last month. The second visit was after your recent visit, and I thank you for going. I heard from members of the community that appreciated your time and your attention up there. I'm keen to understand from you what you heard. What are you hearing as the major issues? What actions are you taking, and what's the Commonwealth doing to address these very serious issues? We, of course, learnt about the 15 children abandoned. We heard about the lack of action and reaction to the Hawke children case. Last week, I met with Dorothy Papertalk, a wonderful grandmother that is still grieving. As soon as I walked into her home, she burst into tears after many years of dealing with the struggle. I'm just keen to understand what you heard and what specific actions Commonwealth has taken.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I certainly met with a number of elders, probably similar to the ones you met with, and a number of organisations. Julyardi was one of those organisations. I was also talking to some of the young people in terms of YIC and the evening program and listening to some of the families. One of the things that struck me immediately was around food and access to food in terms of some of the areas that I have responsibility for. In terms of some of the issues raised more broadly around the care and protection of children, that is something that I've spoken about to the WA minister but also the Children's Commissioner. Clearly, there are steps now underway to look at what they can do in terms of some of those issues raised directly there with those organisations. What we're doing is looking at what we can do at the Commonwealth level in terms of nutrition, food access and the funding that's going into places not just in Port Hedland but in the region. These are the things that we're doing.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: On food security, what specific action have you taken? There's a Coles. There's a McDonald's. There's a Subway. There's a Chicken Treat. There's plenty of access to food. Is it an affordability issue?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: From the conversations I had, it was more around the affordability. One of the organisations that I spoke to has its own store at the front of the organisation, just a small shopfront. Their outreach to the communities nearby was raised with me in terms of wanting to assist those communities. We talked about the food security policy that we have with remote stores and how we rolled out cheaper prices in around 120 stores. Those particular communities that are identified around Port Hedland—my understanding is that they don't have stores. I haven't been to those communities, but I wanted to understand from that organisation what their outreach is and whether there is a possibility that we could look at any kind of support for them, given that Port Hedland is not considered remote. These are a couple of things that we're working on at the moment.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: What I heard was that the community is really looking for leadership, accepting that issues of law and order and child protection are state matters. What they are looking for is leadership. They don't, frankly, care about jurisdictional responsibilities or boundaries. We've got high levels of drug abuse. I heard stories of paedophilia. I heard stories of child-on-child sexual abuse—absolutely horrific, sobering discussions. These problems don't exist in a vacuum, and there are Commonwealth responsibilities. The Commonwealth has responsibility for the welfare system, for example, where you've got unaccountable welfare with mutual obligations clearly not being addressed or met and you've got training programs that are not leading to outcomes and jobs. There's a despair that exists. These things don't happen in isolation.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: No.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: There's frustration within these communities that there's not the leadership. Roger Cook is going up there and not meeting with any community people, it was reported in the papers today. What this community is desperately looking for is leadership. What leadership are you taking and what leadership is the Prime Minister taking to help this community deal with this absolutely atrocious situation, where they've got children with STDs?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: There are a couple of areas that you've raised there, Senator O'Sullivan. Immediately, if you know of any reports about paedophilia you need to report those as well to the local police.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It has been.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: This has to be investigated. I think there are some very practical steps that people can take as soon as they're aware of any of these issues. In terms of the rise in drugs, again, the same thing—that is something that should be directed to policing and law and order.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: They're well aware of it.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We have, in terms of the First Nations children's commissioner, a rapid review underway right now, as we speak, and our government is looking to that leadership with Commissioner Hunter to provide that guidance to us. That is why we created this position of the National Commission for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children in this country, and we do look forward to Commissioner Hunter's work on this. Her rapid review, as she has reassured us, is going to be done very, very swiftly, and so we expect to be guided by that, on evidence bases.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you, Minister. This is the final question from me. Roger Cook, Premier of Western Australia, said that he was going to go there. It was reported in the Australian today that he's not meeting with community people. Is the Prime Minister going to go to Port Hedland to hear these firsthand accounts from people that are dealing with the ravages of so many issues within this community, which you encountered when you were there a few weeks ago?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Senator O'Sullivan, it's really important if the Premier of WA is going to Port Hedland. If he's going there, that is good. It's good to hear.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Should he meet with local people, not just the organisations?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I expect that he will know who he should meet with, and I'm sure you can have that direct conversation with him. In terms of the Commonwealth, though, I must stress the importance of this position, of our national children's commissioner, doing her job, doing what we want her to do. That's why we established this position. The Prime Minister or ministers will be guided by what the children's commissioner provides in her rapid review.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It's not important enough for the Prime Minister to witness it for himself, as our national leader?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Senator O'Sullivan, you're looking for a really nice grab here. Can I say that we are waiting for the children's commissioner's rapid review.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: The children are looking for leadership, Minister. Thank you.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I just want to return to the topic I raised a little while ago. Minister, are you aware that Caxton community legal service, which apparently is funded in part by the Commonwealth government and receives grants, pays First Nations staff a colonial loading payment of four per cent on top of base salary?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: What was the first name you said there, Senator Roberts?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Colonial loading.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: No, the organisation.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Caxton community legal service.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Where is that located?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Brisbane.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: And that is a private company, a private business?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: According to SEEK, it's advertising this condition—Caxton legal service.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Senator Roberts, I'm responsible for the work that our agency does with First Nations organisations across the country. I'm not familiar with the legal service that you're referring to. I can certainly point out, as we've answered to previous questions from you, that if people have any issues with their workplace they can perhaps go to their unions.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We're concerned that taxpayer money is being used to fund this, which is—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Senator Roberts, maybe just to give a bit of guidance here, can you give us the legal status of the organisation that you're referencing? You're calling it taxpayer funded.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It's a community legal service that we believe receives money in part from the Commonwealth government.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Do you know what for?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Through services and also through grants. That's what we believe. So I'd like the minister to check up on that and confirm it.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Senator Roberts, given that you're not clear on the details, I'm not sure that you can expect the minister to be clear on the details either. If you want to put a case study or a scenario, then I think some more detail may be required to enable the minister to answer.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I understand that, Chair. I'd like to know if the minister can assure me that money is not being spent on a racist, biased organisation.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I am not familiar with this organisation.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Well, could you make yourself familiar, please.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: And community legal services do not come under the purview of my responsibilities. It's the Attorney-General.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Okay. If you don't want to, we will. We'll do the research.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: No, no, excuse me—
