agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Are you aware—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Can everyone just calm down. Senator Roberts, I ask you to be a little bit more respectful, if you don't mind. If you're putting a case to a minister and you don't have the details, then I don't think you've really got the right to then start to be aggressive towards that minister.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I'm not being aggressive. I'm adopting—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: That's how I'm interpreting it, Senator Roberts.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: That may be your interpretation, but I'm adopting your position, where you suggested that I do the research. We will.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Great.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: But, Senator Roberts, even though community legal services don't come under the Indigenous Australians portfolio, can I suggest that you put that question to Attorney-General's.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Certainly. What about universities—specifically, the University of Wollongong? Do they have something similar to a colonial loading payment?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We are not responsible for the University of Wollongong.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: So you're not aware?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We're not responsible for the university—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Neither you nor the NIAA are aware of these cultural leave loadings?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: No.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you. That's all I need to know.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Senator Shoebridge.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thanks, everyone, for your attendance. Minister, one of the most troubling things that are happening in the space of youth justice at the moment is the practice of the Northern Territory government of putting spit hoods back on young people who are in detention. Overwhelmingly, that's on First Nations young people. What's your agency doing to understand the extent to which the NT is doing that, and what's the extent to which you are seeking, I hope, to stop it?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: I will refer it to the agency in a moment. It is of great concern in terms of what's happening with the incarceration of First Nations people, in particular in the Northern Territory. And what has added to that concern is the removal of the justice groups in the Northern Territory at this point, with the Northern Territory government and the Northern Territory Attorney-General. We have in three to four weeks time our Joint Council on Closing the Gap, and it will be an important focus. But I'll just refer it to Ms Bellenger.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Senator Shoebridge, it's certainly something we take up in all of the different forums that we have with the Northern Territory government. AGD's lead the national partnership on justice work. They have all of the ministers there from the different Attorney-General offices, and it's definitely been a key issue in that forum as well.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It's not just their continued use of spit hoods. It's the removal of detention as a last resort, which has seen a huge surge of First Nations young people being put into incarceration, overwhelming many of the legal supports that are in place and that are pretty much all funded by the Commonwealth. Again I ask what this department is doing in response to that.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: The majority of the funding sits with Attorney-General's, and they'd be best placed. In terms of what our agency does, though, we do fund the through-care system through NAAJA—we regularly meet with them—and we've got different systems of support in remote communities to try to avoid people coming into detention in the first place. Attorney-General's, though, are largely responsible for the funding of the justice and legal systems.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Yes. I asked Attorney-General's earlier today, and they largely said, 'The criminal justice system is a matter for the states and territories. It's on SCAG,' which is the Standing Council of Attorneys-General. But it's been on SCAG now for a decade. I think this is target 11 in Closing the Gap and doesn't seem to change. Well, it doesn't seem to change for the good; it's changing for the worse. What's happening in the NT is mirrored in Queensland to some extent and in New South Wales. The Attorney-General's response is. 'That's what states and territories do.' That's not an answer, do you think, Minister?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It is an answer.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Well, it's not a valid answer.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It is an answer, and it is a legitimate answer. The difficulty, though, is that it's not changing.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Well, it is changing. It's getting worse. The NT government—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It's not changing for the better, is what I am referring to when I say it's not changing. It's not changing for the better, and that is the challenge for us.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: But you've been given advice—I think, through the ALS and NAAJA—from two incredibly well-respected lawyers, one a highly respected silk and the other a senior junior, saying the Commonwealth has the ability to legislate in this place. You can use the external affairs power. You can legislate to actually prevent this kind of abuse happening. Are these discussions happening at all inside your government, Minister?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: The Commonwealth does have powers. It has tremendous powers, certainly as far as the Northern Territory is concerned. But—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: To be clear, their advice was not using the Territory's power. This advice was using the external affairs power and was focused on that because of the very real concerns about using the Territory's powers. Could I ask you to focus on that?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Well, I would put this to you: that belongs to the Attorney-General, and perhaps you focus on that.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Well, you see, Minister, one of the frustrations I think many people have in the way your government is structured is that you, as the minister responsible for Indigenous Australians are in charge of NIAA, which is the agency which has front and centre, at least external responsibility. I don't doubt that there's goodwill inside your department. I don't doubt there's goodwill with you, Minister. I don't doubt this, but what I see is the agency, which is branded as the one supporting First Nations people, doesn't seem to have the power. All the power lies with the Attorney-General's Department or Finance or Treasury, and you're here answering questions, but you're not. None of the levers are given to you to fix things. It must be incredibly frustrating.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: It's very frustrating, Senator Shoebridge, when we have the National Agreement on Closing the Gap, and, yes, target 11 is going backwards. That is incredibly frustrating, yes.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: There was a recommendation out of a Senate committee, barely a few weeks ago, calling for the establishment of a national taskforce to address this. Where does responsibility to answer those recommendations lie in terms of ministerial responsibility? Does it lie with you? Does it lie with the Attorney—

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: That would be with the A-G.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: When these matters cut so obviously across your responsibilities, is there a process where you come together and try and provide a joint response? How does this work?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Well, there certainly will be a process of coming together, which often occurs with most of the reports that come to the Senate and any that I've had any involvement with. That will be an ongoing conversation as to when we finalise the responses to any report.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: One of the statements you made a couple of months ago was about looking at funding levers in order to produce positive outcomes. In relation to the NT, the Commonwealth funds 80 per cent of their budget, and that's probably on a good day for them. It's probably more than that on some other days. And yet they continue to defy the Commonwealth in their agenda of punching down on young people, ignoring the Closing the Gap, ignoring the goals that they've signed up to on national agreements. What is the state of play in terms of using those funding levers?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We've certainly spoken with the Northern Territory government—the finance minister and I. We've sat down with them to express our real concerns at the federal level in terms of the funding arrangements across all areas, particularly a number that were standing out quite recently—that is with housing and homelessness and also with the emergency disaster relief. We were nearly a year from when the first disaster hit, and applications even for that had not come in. It has now, but only after or just before we had the meeting. The timeliness of those sorts of things was raised but also the reality that we would consider direct funding to Aboriginal organisations and local government. We have raised that directly with the Northern Territory government. That's if they don't lift their game. And this has been a serious conversation between the Commonwealth and the Northern Territory.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: And can I urge you, on behalf of my party, to progress that, because it would appear that we have a level of government in the Northern Territory which seems to want to weaponise the justice system against First Nations peoples and weaponise the justice system against First Nations youth, comprehensively failing in its basic duties to the citizens of the NT to ensure that emergency funding is delivered so their lives can be improved after disasters and comprehensively failing to deliver the housing support that they've been funded to do. And when a level of government so comprehensively fails to do its basic duties and then, with the money that has been provided to them, is engaged in an overtly noxious political campaign against First Nations peoples, this surely is the moment in which to say, 'Well, if you won't do what's right with Commonwealth funds, we'll find organisations and other places which will do the right thing with the Commonwealth funds.' Is that the conversation you're having with them?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Absolutely. What we also have to be very, very cognisant of is capability of our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander organisations to actually take it on. And so that's another level which I'm very firm on—that we do not want our organisations to fail, either. The capability factor is really critical whilst having these very solid, direct conversations with the Northern Territory government. But it's not just the Northern Territory government. It is other governments too. We are making this quite an important focus for us, if we are not getting the outcomes we want to see.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Yes.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: If it's helpful—for the funding agreements and funding arrangements that sit in the minister's portfolio, including the NTRAI, which Ms Bellenger spoke to earlier, we have put in measures to ensure that we are paying for services rendered. If those services are not provided by the Northern Territory government as the partner, then those payments won't be made. We've put in greater Aboriginal community oversight under those partnership arrangements. In relation to the remote housing agreement, which the minister has responsibility for, that is under its periodic two-year review, and we are looking at again strengthening those and what other partners exist to deliver those services under those agreements.
witness_organisation: National Indigenous Australians Agency
witness_position: Deputy Chief Executive Officer, Policy and Programs

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thanks, I appreciate that. Minister, I hear repeatedly about capacity building and the need for capacity building in First Nations communities. This is something that I would have thought your department could take a national lead on—to create a funding stream and a support stream and an education stream and a training stream so that people in these remote communities and in First Nations organisations are getting the training now, so that, in 18 months or two years time, there's a capacity there to redirect the funding. Is that a project? Is it funded? To what scale is it happening? Or is this a budget request coming forward?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: We've certainly focused on the Northern Territory in terms of capability. I know Ms Bellenger responded to earlier questions on NTRAI just in regards to a certain amount of funding that's gone directly to Aboriginal organisations through APO NT to ensure capability and to make sure that we continue to build these ACCOs across the Territory. I do want to see that right across the country. It's not just about the Northern Territory, and I'm very mindful of that. However, the most pressing matters seem to be coming from northern Australia, at this point in time, more broadly.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Because the chair has been very indulgent and nice, could I ask you to provide that detail about training, capacity building and funding on notice with as much granularity as you can?

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Sure.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thanks, Minister.

agency: National Indigenous Australians Agency
text: Thank you for your time. Apologies to everyone for the blowout in the agenda. We are a number of hours behind, and we're doing our best. We will let you go. Thank you so much for your time.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: There is the Central Land Council. Welcome. It's very good to see you.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Sort of!

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: It's very good to squint in your general direction! Thank you so much for joining us. We really apologise for the delay. I believe we have Anindilyakwa online as well—yes, there you are. While the other land councils are making their way to the room and joining us at the table, I will ask the Central Land Council to start and provide any opening statement that you may have.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: We do have an opening statement if that suits the committee.
witness_organisation: Central Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Yes. Do you want to go straight ahead?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text:
Yes, thank you. First, in regard to the shocking news on Helen Haines, our thoughts are with her and her family. Hello, Madam Chair and committee members. We at the Central Land Council appreciate the opportunity to attend these estimates hearings and answer your questions. We're committed to good governance and welcome the important role of the Senate estimates in ensuring public accountability. Thank you for agreeing to us appearing virtually today.

Last week or the week before was Anti-Poverty Week in Australia. Some of you may have met with a small CLC delegation who travelled to Canberra to talk to lawmakers about the conditions our constituents face in Central Australia. Our people are struggling to survive amid soaring prices for fuel and household goods. The grinding poverty that Aboriginal people continue to experience over generations impacts all facets of people's lives, not only in the difficulty of affording fuel and household goods but also by straining emotional and social wellbeing. Poverty traps people in the struggle to survive from day to day and deprives them of the ability to plan for a better future.

For remote communities to succeed, they need decent housing, education, health services, affordable food and transport, community safety and employment opportunities. Without these essential foundations, how can they maintain a basic economy and envision a future which most other Australians enjoy? In remote communities, living costs are 40 per cent higher than in the nearest towns. Kids are going hungry. People can't afford to keep their power on over the long, hot desert summers or warm themselves in the winter. Conditions are dangerous for the elderly, babies and infants and make food storage and cooling almost impossible. It's well past the time to address the inequity that Aboriginal people in remote communities experience. Thank you.
witness_organisation: Central Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Thank you very much. We really appreciate your time. We'll go to Anindilyakwa online as well. If you would like to proceed to any opening statement, that would be great.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text:
Okay. I'll just go straight to the opening statement. Madam Chair and senators, I'd like to acknowledge and pay my respects to the Ngunnawal and Ngambri people and elders past and present, the First Nations of the land on which the committee is meeting. The Anindilyakwa Land Council is attending from the lands of the traditional owners of the Groote archipelago. Our chair, Ms Wurrawilya, gives her apologies today; she is sorry she cannot join us here today.

With Kupa Teao's commencement as CEO, key areas of the ALC operations and community priorities have reached much-needed attention. Community control and local decision-making continues to be a focus for the traditional owners to increase and control the matters that impact our communities. There is a major focus on preparing for mine closure and involving community in the process of planning and growing a sustainable future post GEMCO's mine closure. We are committed to working together with stakeholders, applying sound governance practices and keeping focus on the task ahead of us to reach positive outcomes for our community.

I will now pass to our CEO, Kupa Teao, to say a few brief words. This is Kupa's first address to the committee as ALC CEO.
witness_organisation: Anindilyakwa Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text:
I'd like to echo the acknowledgement of country on which the parliament stands—the Ngunnawal and Ngambri people. I'd like to acknowledge elders past and present. I'd also like to acknowledge the Anindilyakwa people, whose country we are reaching the Senate estimates hearing from. I pay my respect to elders past and present. I am deeply honoured by the Anindilyakwa Land Council board, the ALC board, having the confidence in me in my appointment as their CEO.

Since arriving on country in February of this year, I've gained a deeper appreciation, respect and understanding of the country's beauty and of the Indigenous community's connection to it. The ALC's vision is to assist its community by promoting a future economy that is sustainable and inclusive. This can only be achieved by empowering the community through a multifaceted approach.

In addition to adopting a holistic community consultation process, my focus has been on stakeholder engagements and structured collaboration to build trust and align expectations to improve strategic outcomes. I am pleased to be attending today and welcome your questions.
witness_organisation: Anindilyakwa Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Welcome; we're delighted to have you with us today. And congratulations on your appointment. We'll now move on to the Northern Land Council.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text:
If I may, I want to acknowledge the Ngunnawal and Ngambri people, on whose lands we stand today, and recognise that their sovereignty over these lands was never ceded. This always was and always will be Aboriginal land.

It's been 50 years since the Aboriginal land rights act was passed. In the five decades since, the northern, central, Tiwi and Anindilyakwa land councils have played a pivotal part in returning land, advocating for and assisting traditional owners to acquire and manage their lands and seas. The Northern Land Council is committed to strongly advocating for Aboriginal people in the Top End to acquire and manage their traditional lands and seas through the exercise of these and other rights that have emerged over this time. Our vision is for a Territory where the rights and responsibilities of traditional owners are not only recognised but respected and held with a level of authority. Aboriginal people should be able to not only have ownership of their land and seas but benefit economically, socially and culturally.

Senators, 2026 has brought significant challenges for our 51,000 constituents, but there have also been important achievements. In recent months, the Northern Land Council's Water Committee and its Housing and Homelands Committee came together for the first time, producing a powerful joint statement calling on all levels of government to take real action on the poor quality of essential services in remote communities. For too long, essential services in remote communities have been in the too-hard basket for successive governments. Improving essential services in the region must no longer be an afterthought.

In Bulla community, west of Katherine, residents are unable to drink the tap water due to unsafe levels of barium, and, in Daly River, a community hit with unprecedented flooding at the beginning of this year, pallets of bottled water are being dropped off each week due to the water being deemed unsafe. We are continuing to raise the alarm on this issue and amplify the voices of our traditional owners, who are often overlooked on these matters.

In a win for Aboriginal managed land, the South-East Arnhem Land Indigenous Protected Area officially acquired over 80,000 hectares of sea country, making it the largest marine area under Aboriginal management in the Northern Territory. This dedication was years in the making and was thanks to the strength and determination of past and current SEAL IPA members, traditional owners and NLC staff.

For the last few years, the NLC has supported the decision by native title holders to negotiate an appraisal agreement that allows the Beetaloo joint venture to sell up to 60 terajoules of gas per day over a period of three years. This agreement will mean a number of positive outcomes that will see jobs and benefits for native title holders. Traditional owners want an active role in what happens on their country and are looking forward to growth and investment in local communities and in the township of Elliott. Genuine partnership with traditional owners is key for economic growth for the whole Territory.

NLC's Learning on Country Program continues to grow from strength to strength. In October, it was announced that the program is expanding from 14 to 18 remote community school sites, creating new opportunities for Aboriginal students to engage in on-country learning, strengthen cultural knowledge and explore pathways to further education, training and employment. This significant expansion will formally welcome the Nawarddeken Academy schools at Mamadawerre, Manmoyi and Kabulwarnamyo homelands into the program in partnership with Warddeken Land Management, alongside Bulman-Weemol School in partnership with Mimal Land Management. It is expected to engage an additional 90 to 115 middle and senior secondary students each year while creating part-time employment opportunities for approximately 35 to 50 local cultural educators and community members.

As we head towards the end of a 2026 that has been both challenging and rewarding, we reflect on what has been achieved and on the work still ahead of us.
witness_organisation: Northern Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Thank you very much. Tiwi Land Council—Mr Toy.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: I'll just introduce other members and staff that we've got here. We've got Mr Austin Wonaeamirri, chairman of the Tiwi Land Council; Ms Karina Coombes, who's the trustee for the Munupi landowning clan group on Tiwi; Ms Ana Garcia, who's our governance and risk officer; and Ms Suzanne Munkara, another Tiwi person, who's working in our Closing the Gap policy officer space. We'll bounce a little bit, but I'll hand over to the chair to start to do his bit of the opening statement, and I'll finish off.
witness_organisation: Tiwi Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text:
Firstly, we'd like to acknowledge the Ngunnawal and Ngambri peoples, the traditional owners of this land we meet on. Thank you for the opportunity to appear today on behalf of the Tiwi Land Council. In this opening statement, I would like to share two examples of the critical work our land council is doing to keep our Tiwi culture strong. Firstly, we have been doing strategic planning for Tiwi homelands. Homelands are the foundation of our identity, culture and wellbeing. We are talking about this now because, over the next few months, the Australian and Tiwi governments will be making decisions about future investments in homelands. Homelands have been neglected by government for a very long time. It was really good to see the Australian government start putting money back into homelands in 2022. This money runs out in the middle of next year. Tiwi people have plans for their homelands. They are places for respite and healing. They are places for passing on knowledge and keeping culture strong. They are also places where we can share our culture with visitors through tourism and create jobs for Tiwi people while staying connected to country.

The aspirations that Tiwi people have identified are practical and achievable, but they need investment. Tiwi people are already working on ways to generate our own income to support homeland living. For example, some homelands' businesses are already established, like the momentous cross-cultural camps at Pitjiramirra on Melville Island. There are other plans for more, including the Mapurlarri Prawn Farm at Ranku on Bathurst Island and the ecotourism at Taracumbie on Melville Island. What we also need is support from the government to fund the basic infrastructure that keeps homelands alive. The homelands movement hasn't gone away. Tiwi people are living on and returning to homelands. We have seen how the recent Homelands Housing and Infrastructure Program, HHIP, investment has enabled families to return at places like Taracumbie and Conder Point. We encourage the federal government to see the opportunity that comes from investments in homelands as places of cultural importance, physical and spiritual health and economic opportunity. I will now hand over to our CEO, Brenton Toy, to discuss some of our operations.
witness_organisation: Tiwi Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text:
This is just one example. The Tiwi Land Council recognises the critical importance of investing in and maintaining a strong cultural land rights system. To support this work, the land council has formally established the Tuwurrampila Cultural Committee as a formal subcommittee of the land council. We've done this because we know that cultural maintenance and revitalisation is not just a nice thing for the land council to do; it's central to effective land governance because effective land governance relies on cultural authority.

I will share an experience that our culture committee had recently—stories about truth-telling, healing and cultural authority. In September, they went for a visit down to the South Australian Museum, and, a week out from attending the museum, they were advised that there are 23 ancestral remains still held at the museum. It is a bit of a shock to Tiwi people to know that there are bones sitting in places that we don't even know about. Our committee had the opportunity to go and view these remains and have the conversation with the SA Museum. As you can imagine, this was a profoundly moving experience for our members. Following on from the museum visit, the next month our culture committee just spent going back to community, talking about the experience and letting them know about the remains, and I've never seen our clan group so engaged in a conversation, to get a sense of the importance of the ancestors and our connection to our history. During October, our culture committee went out and shared the experience of their visit with the SA Museum, connecting with our clans, talking about our ancestors, and it's clear that Tiwi people want our ancestors to be brought home. For the Tiwi Land Council and Tiwi people, repatriation is not simply the return of ancestral remains; it is the return of Tiwi authority over those remains and the responsibility for what happens to them in the future. It is healing. It is recognising and making peace with our past. It's history and knowledge that we can carry forward through our current and future generations. This is important work of the Tiwi Land Council's culture committee, and it's something that we want to continue to take forward. Thank you.
witness_organisation: Tiwi Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Thank you very much. We really appreciate it. We will go to Senator Shoebridge, but can I first ask: with that repatriation, what is the process that is open to you at this point in time?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Most places have been very good. I access the museums, and we're having that conversation to say that we really need a central authority to decide what happens to that, and we're agreeing that the land council is that group. There are a few things involved in it. We can repatriate remains, but we need an appropriate storage place for them. That's the first thing. What we're doing is getting out and finding out where these things are and then agreeing that the authority for where they sit sits with the land council. And then we have conversations around: well, what things can we return? Digital collections—no worries, we can do that. But the hard artefacts—some of them are hundreds of years old and very brittle and need to be kept in climate controlled environments. For us, first, it's establishing the authority—that the Tiwi Land Council decides what happens to them. If we say we want it to stay in the SA Museum, then that's what it does. It's establishment of cultural authority and working out what things we want to bring back. The whole point of talking to our clan groups is that some of the remains aren't identifiable, so getting DNA testing to try and find descendants of the ancestors of those remains I think is a step as well. But then it's the conversation around: what do we do with them? Do we keep them in storage? There are some families that go, 'No, no; part of our ceremony way is to have a funeral and ceremony and send them off properly, so that that spirit of that person can leave this world.' To step that out, it's establishing the cultural authority, getting identification around the descendants through DNA testing and then working out what the appropriate storage mechanism might be. Aside to that is the work that we're doing with the different groups to try and find an appropriate storage facility, which might mean combining and talking about cyclone preparedness—like a cyclone shelter that doubles as a cultural holding place for us as well.
witness_organisation: Tiwi Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Thank you very much. We'll go to Senator Shoebridge.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Being creative about making both a keeping place and a protection place—keeping those kinds of ideas coming forward from Tiwi Land Council—is incredibly important work. Thank you for doing what you do to make sure you're protecting that history and protecting those remains. It's incredibly important. I also just want to acknowledge the extraordinary work of Northern Land Council. I think that's 800,000 hectares of First Nations managed marine lands. I know you spoke about it for about 30 seconds, but I just want to acknowledge the decade-plus of work that's gone into that and the incredible achievements. To the extent possible, can I just ask you to pass on the gratitude for probably a generation of people who have done that work and seen it finally come to fruition. It's extraordinary.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Thanks.
witness_organisation: Tiwi Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Can I also say to our friends from Groote and Anindilyakwa Land Council, we had the great privilege to go onto your country, and you were incredibly generous hosts to the Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee. You showed us your beautiful country, and can I just give my incredible appreciation for some of the work you've been doing there, including the 32-bed Healing Centre. I might ask you to just briefly tell this committee about some of the incredible work you're doing preventing people getting caught up in the criminal justice system, instead dealing with them with healing on country. Could you briefly tell us about that?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Thank you, Senator Shoebridge. It was a privilege to have you and the other committee members come onto country. I'm going to pass some time over to traditional owner, Matty McKenzie, because he's on the Community Justice Group. But before I pass the time over to him, it is one of numerous programs we have on Groote Island, which is a huge success story. I'm deeply, deeply proud of the Community Justice Group program. The success of that program is the face-to-face game, going into the families and the case manager, defendants understanding what brought them to that particular situation. Then, the cream on the top is, as you rightly put it, is the healing centre. We're hoping we can replicate that program in other areas. I'll pass some time over to Matty McKenzie.
witness_organisation: Anindilyakwa Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: I'm actually the founder of the program, Community Justice Group. I've been on the program for quite a while now. Regarding the Anindilyakwa Healing Centre, I actually oversee that. The reason why we actually built that on our own land is that it's about bringing our people to do their time in their own country. It has 32 beds, but at the moment we have about 10 inmates. It's a lot cheaper than bringing our people here to attend a family's funeral. Sometimes it's costing us nearly over 10 grand to bring our people here to attend a family's funeral.
witness_organisation: Anindilyakwa Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: And if I could add, Senator, it's the healing power of country. These are programs that are owned and delivered by traditional owners for their people.
witness_organisation: Anindilyakwa Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text:
Yes. Can I say that all of that work on country and preventing people being taken off the island and being sucked up into the criminal justice system—every time you do that, it's a cultural win. I really want to thank you for it.

I do have some questions to the Central Land Council. The first is about the Bush Bus. The NT infrastructure minister said that the Bush Bus missed out on 25-26 funding. My understanding is that this means that there are at least five of their routes that are not being operated. What's been the impact of that, and what are you asking for?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: We were made aware of the cut to the Bush Bus service by the Northern Territory government and by the owners of Bush Bus. We actually found out through a meeting at the hospital. In terms of the concerns we have, it's the most equitable and efficient transport service, and the subsidy was working. In terms of the community, it misses out on transport of constituents into town to meet with doctors, hospital appointments, and for food. It also delivers freight and medicines out to communities. We also learnt that the NT government had cut the subsidy on those routes that you mentioned, and we have written to the Treasurer of the Northern Territory government asking for that to be reinstated. We have not heard back from the Treasurer. We've also raised our concerns in the Northern Territory parliament.
witness_organisation: Central Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Minister, have you heard about the cancellation of these Bush Bus services, the five routes for the Bush Bus? My understanding is that people can't get food, and people can't get family connected. It's creating difficulties in the justice system. They seem to me to be really critical services that have been ripped out of these communities.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Yes, I am aware of it. I have certainly seen the news on it. I haven't been approached directly, from my understanding, in terms of any letters or direct contact with me, but I am very aware of it. I have asked for my agency and Central Australia to keep an eye on that and see what we can do.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Has any of the money that the NT government had in the remote transport program budget, which I think was about $3.1 million, come from the Commonwealth, and are you willing to look to that as to whether or not, if the NT government is unwilling to provide it to the bush bus—we spoke earlier about direct funding. Is this a case for direct funding?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: We provide, through the NTRAI, a significant amount of funding. I would have to take on notice how that's broken down in terms of the bush bus, and I'm happy to take that.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: I heard through the CLC—and maybe the CLC could give some details about this—about people being basically abandoned in Alice Springs after they've gone to see a doctor, with no way home. The overcrowding that's already endemic in some of those family homes has been further aggravated because of the cancellation of the bush bus. Is that happening?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Yes, that's correct. Also, in terms of the accommodation, when people are stuck in town, it's stretching Aboriginal hostels—their transient hostels. In terms of Corrections, people are just being dropped off in town as well, with no service to deliver people back home, back onto country. The bush bus served that purpose. It's an issue that we continue to raise with the Northern Territory government.
witness_organisation: Central Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Minister, given what we've heard again from the Central Land Council, I ask you: will you directly raise that with the NT government now, and go through that process to see if any of that funding that was previously allocated for the remote transport program budget has been Commonwealth funding?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: We will be asking that question, but we already have been, through the infrastructure minister here at the Commonwealth level, and the Northern Territory government. We're very concerned. As I've said previously, that's why we went to meet with the Northern Territory government, with the finance minister.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Yes, but I stress that, in relation to the bush bus, as we've just heard its impact is happening now. Delays in getting it restarted—because the Northern Territory government has been bloody-minded—are having these very real human impacts on a daily basis. Will it be addressed with that urgency in mind, Minister?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: There is a lot of urgency on a lot of levels, Senator Shoebridge, and they are being dealt with, yes.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Thank you. Minister, could I ask you about the remote area allowance. I think it's still $9.10 a week for a single person, and the last increase was a grand total of 35c and it was 25 years ago. What does $1.30 a day actually buy you in remote areas? It doesn't seem to come close to dealing with the additional costs in housing, food, energy, water, clothing, living.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: It's really difficult. We had the Central Land Council down here just recently talking with us about it. Both Marion Scrymgour and I met with Dr Douglas, and others who came from the outstations, and representatives from the Central Land Council, and they're very concerned. We have raised that. What we know is that we can't move on it at this point in time. I've been looking at other areas like the food security program and the policies that we're trying to roll out in our stores across not only the Northern Territory but other remote areas of Australia. That food security policy is about the reduction of prices in the stores. So we are very mindful of the pressures on people living remote.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: When you say it can't be done at this point, what does that mean? Is that code for something?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: No, it's not code for anything. It just can't be done right now. I don't have the responsibility of it. It's something that—

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Who does?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Minister Plibersek has responsibility for this particular area. The advocacy of both the Central Land Council and others has been very firm in regard to pointing out those issues.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Can I ask the CLC, the Central Land Council. You've done the numbers and you've tried to work out what the remote area allowance would need to rise to to meet what it was meeting decades ago, when it was first set. Have you got a figure, and can you tell us what it is?

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: CLC, along with others across Australia, are calling for the remote area allowance to be increased to $121.30 a week. That would be an increase of $17.30 a day for a single adult. This represents a 30 per cent increase in the overall value of a single JobSeeker payment and it's pitched at 30 per cent, even though we know that the cost of living for remote is 40 per cent. The 30 per cent does take into account the 30 items in the remote essentials subsidy, which is very welcome. It's pragmatic number crunching and it goes to providing a targeted measure for cost-of-living relief for people living in remote and very remote Australia.
witness_organisation: Central Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: I know we're running behind time. That's my final question. Can I thank all of you for all the work you do. I really appreciate it. Minister, I ask you to raise again with your ministerial colleagues the urgency of this remote area allowance lift.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: We do advocate and will continue to do so.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: We'll go with one last roll for Senator Walker, and then we will go to the break.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: The Northern Land Council, I understand that you run Indigenous rangers programs, which are funded by the Commonwealth. I really enjoy hearing about a lot of the successes that come out of that program. Can you step me through some of the benefits of these programs for people living on country.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text:
The rangers program, as you've rightly pointed out, is funded under the Caring for Country funding envelope. Just as a bit of background, the Caring for Country program was established in 1995 and was an incubator of many of the ranger groups in the top half of the Northern Territory. Many have since left the Caring for Country program to become successful independent Indigenous ranger programs, and Caring for Country currently administers 14 Indigenous ranger groups. I won't run through the 14 for you. But it does provide support for three Indigenous protected areas, and the one that I talked about in my opening statement was the SEAL IPA, or the South East Arnhem Land IPA. We're actually undertaking consultations around a dedicated marine IPA.

In terms of the facts and the figures behind our ranger program, it provides support for 63 full-time-equivalent staff through NIAA funding. The ILSC, the Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation, also provide funding for another 10 FTE, and there's 11 from DCCEEW and another five through our ABA fund. So it's 92 FTE all up in terms of the aggregated amount. It not only includes Indigenous employment; it includes non-Indigenous employment as well. But our program runs at 80 per cent Indigenous employment, and that's predominantly the rangers themselves. Of particular interest is the female representation in the workforce, and that stands at 35 per cent. Gender equity is a continuous focus for the program. We have made significant strides in improving female representation. For example, at the ranger coordinator level, five of our 14 ranger coordinators are Indigenous females. We can benchmark that as an increase from zero in 2021. In terms of the Indigenous Protected Area cohort, three of the four IPA coordinators are female. More broadly, the ranger program not only provides business-as-usual activities on country—caring for country and providing cultural knowledge through the ranger program—but also steps in with regard to emergency responses around floods and other natural disasters. The ranger program also assists in border protection, even though we're not funded for that component. Discussions continue with border protection on how our ranger program can be better equipped and trained for the protection of borders.
witness_organisation: Northern Land Council

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Thank you. Can I also say thank you because I know you've all travelled quite far to be here today. Thank you for doing that. We appreciate it.

agency: Anindilyakwa Land Council Central Land Council Northern Land Council Tiwi Land Council
text: Thank you. There are no further questions. I do really appreciate the time that you take to wait online as we run hideously over time or the time you take to travel down. It really does mean a lot to us. Please always feel free to put in requests to appear online, given that it is very challenging from some of your locations. With that, we will release this outcome area. Thank you so much for your time. We will now take a break, and we will return at 4.55 with the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Good afternoon. I'd like to welcome Senator the Hon. Penny Wong, Minister for Foreign Affairs, representing the Prime Minister; Dr Steven Kennedy, Secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet; and other officers that have joined us. Minister, would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
Yes, I would, thank you. Before we begin the PM&C estimates, I do want to address the horrific attack that occurred on Monday last week against Dr Helen Haines outside her electorate office in Wangaratta. Helen, her husband, Phil, her children, her grandchildren, her team and everyone who loves her are in our thoughts, and we hold them close in our hearts. This is a time of great distress and of great shock. As we meet this afternoon, Helen remains in hospital. It is impossible to comprehend that someone so well loved around this place and around the nation, especially back home in her community, has met with such violence whilst doing her job. There are so many reasons Helen Haines is loved and respected. As a community representative, Helen is dedicated and diligent. She is a serious legislator. Helen is intelligent, driven by integrity and committed to social justice.

In 2022, I had the honour of receiving the McKinnon Prize in political leadership alongside Helen, who was recognised as the McKinnon Emerging Political Leader of the Year. The judges recognised her integrity, her dedication to her community and her remarkable ability to build consensus across parliament, particularly in the establishment of a national integrity commission. When she accepted the award, Helen said it was her community who had spurred her on, and that is Helen: even in the moment of personal recognition, her focus was on the people she serves. Helen sees the best in people. She is generous, a champion of community engagement and a serious campaigner. There is no doubt. What defines Helen's politics is that they are grounded in kindness. Helen Haines does politics with a great deal of grace.

We know all Australians are searching for answers. The Victorian Police, the AFP and ASIO are continuing their investigations, and we thank them for their work. As they continue these investigations, what is clear is that the epidemic of violence against women in this country must end and that the heightened anger, grievance and violence that is beginning to characterise so much of public debate cannot go on. As parliamentarians, we see this regularly but increasingly too so do frontline workers—emergency service workers, retail workers, nurses and many more. Everyone has a right to go to work, to come home safe and to be safe at home.

Many of us have been urging the temperature be lowered for some time, but what does that mean? I think it means everyone who contributes to the public debate, whether in parliament, in the media or in the public square, must all remember that our words have consequences. We must all find a way to disagree respectfully and constructively. We have always had disagreement in Australia. It's part of our story and it's an important part of our democracy. But it is vital that this debate is conducted in a way that lifts our nation up, not one that tears it down. Helen Haines is a shining example of exactly how we can conduct ourselves in this way.

This morning, when Helen's husband, Phil, spoke to members of parliament, he spoke of hope that this tragedy could become the moment that breaks the fever, the moment our country chooses to turn towards a gentler and more cohesive path. I also want to echo the words of the Prime Minister in saying a sincere thank you to the first responders and to those members of the public who assisted on the scene—Australians who ran towards danger. They are heroes. They show us again that at the worst of times we see the best of the Australian character. That is something I know is keeping Helen's team going and something which is giving us all heart as we process this horrific event.

I again send our love to Helen and to her loved ones. Helen, we know you are a fighter and we look forward to seeing you back in this place fighting for your community when the time is right.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you, Minister Wong. Dr Kennedy, would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
Yes, I'd like to make a brief opening statement. I am the Secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet. Other members of the Prime Minister and Cabinet executive are also in attendance for this session. A detailed list of witnesses attending has been provided to the committee secretariat, and I have PM&C's organisation chart available for the committee should you wish for it to be tabled.

I understand the committee wishes to discuss the Secretaries Board submission to the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Parliamentary Standards as part of its inquiry into the operation and effectiveness of behaviour codes and standards in Commonwealth parliamentary workplaces. I'm pleased to be here to answer those questions.

Before I do so, can I express, on behalf of the Australian Public Service, my shock and dismay at what occurred in Wangaratta last Monday. On behalf of the Australian Public Service, we hope the member for Indi's, Dr Helen Haines, recovery is as full and speedy as it can be.

I would also like to make some remarks about the circumstances and views surrounding ministers, parliamentarians and high office holders at this time. Mostly through my career, I have observed a healthy engagement between the public and elected officials, one that, from the public's perspective, can be sceptical but is also respectful, curious and open. Sadly, in more recent years I have seen a substantial lift in unacceptable behaviour directed towards elected officials, especially women. Social media, in my view, has provided a platform for this behaviour. To date and in this regard, social media has not been a virtual public square encouraging informed debate and promoting democracy. It has often been a platform for unacceptable comments and behaviour.

Let me now turn to the Secretaries Board submission. The Secretaries Board is established by section 64 of the Public Service Act. It is comprised of all departmental secretaries, the Australian Public Service Commissioner and such other persons as nominated by the Secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet. Currently, the Chief Executive Officer of the National Indigenous Australians Agency is a member of the board. I am the chair of the board, and the commissioner is the deputy chair. The functions of the board are set out in section 64(3) of the Public Service Act and include taking responsibility for stewardship of the Australian Public Service, considering issues that affect the APS and modelling leadership behaviours.

Secretaries and other senior public officials have a particular responsibility, both legally and ethically, for the health and safety of Australian public servants. This includes a duty to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of public servants while they are at work. The board is concerned that some conduct during committee hearings may put at risk the health of public servants appearing as witnesses and may consequently engage the duties of senior officials and parliamentarians under the Work Health and Safety Act. We have set out some examples of conduct we are concerned about in our submission, including examples where individual public servants have been accused of engaging in criminal conduct, being racist, gross violations of human rights and engaging in acts deliberately intended to harm others.

In our view, conduct that demeans, intimidates, humiliates or personally targets witnesses is inconsistent with the expectations established by the behaviour standards and behaviour code. Section 7 of the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians provides that parliamentarians must treat all those with whom they come into contact in the course of their parliamentary duties and activities with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect. Similarly, the behaviour standards note that people in parliamentary workplaces must act respectfully and professionally. As the committee is aware, the behaviour code goes on to state in section 8 that parliamentarians, as employers and leaders in the community, have a leading role to play in fostering a healthy, safe, respectful and inclusive environment where all people feel safe and valued. The behaviour standards note that people in parliamentary workplaces must uphold laws that support safe and respectful workplaces, including work, health and safety laws.

Of course, this is not a one-way street. It is incumbent on all public servants to be aware of and act in accordance with their obligations under the APS values and code of conduct as established under the Public Service Act. When appearing before parliamentary committees, public servants should familiarise themselves with the Government Guidelines for Official Witnesses before Parliamentary Committees and Related Matters, which are intended to assist in the freest possible flow of information to the parliament. To that end, the guidelines provide that public servants appearing before parliamentary committees should be open, respectful and courteous.

It is now common practice for many parliamentarians to broadcast interactions with public servants appearing before committees through social media. Secretaries understand the importance of parliamentarians being able to reach their constituencies by whatever means is most effective. As the committee knows, the Senate provides for the broadcasting of proceedings of a committee for the purposes only of making fair and accurate reports of those proceedings. The board is concerned that broadcasts by parliamentarians may not always be fair and accurate reports of what has occurred before a committee. We are aware of examples where, in our view, evidence has been truncated or taken out of context in ways that misrepresent what occurred or would likely be misleading to the public. We are also aware of examples where evidence has been edited in ways that invite ridicule, hostility or abuse directed at individual public servants. We do not ask that public servants be shielded from fair or accurate reporting of what has been said before a committee, nor that we become the arbiters of these issues. However, in response to a parliamentary committee inquiry which seeks views on all these matters, we thought it would be useful for the inquiry to hear our views and observations.

Moreover, an unfortunate feature of social media is that it provides an all-too-easy platform for those who would espouse misogynistic, racist or violent views. Unfortunately, some public servants have been the subject of vile abuse and threats online in response to clips made by parliamentarians. We give some examples of this type of abuse in the submission. Public servants quickly become aware when they are subject to this kind of abuse, be that through their own social media use, through colleagues or through family and friends.

We do not ask that parliamentarians desist from fair and accurate reporting of what has been said before a committee, but we would ask that they take reasonable steps to moderate comments and messages and to remove abusive or otherwise harmful responses. We are aware of some parliamentarians who have done this when alerted to the existence of such commentary, and this is greatly appreciated. Finally, I would note that secretaries have observed that it is often female public servants and those from First Nations and CALD backgrounds who experience the more egregious forms of abuse on social media.

In closing, secretaries welcome the resolution agreed to by the Senate on 9 September regarding the broadcast and publication of proceedings. The resolution sets out clearly the responsibilities and powers of senators and the Senate and the accountabilities of public servants. As our submission states, committee hearings are intended to facilitate robust examination of government administration, expenditure and performance. Public confidence in both parliament and official witnesses is best served when those proceedings are rigorous, robust and respectful. Thank you for the opportunity to provide an opening statement. I look forward to the questions.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you, Dr Kennedy. Just for the process, we are running behind. Dr Kennedy is with us for an hour as per Senate order. I would also note that Minister Wong needs to leave at six, and we will be subbing in Minister Ayres between six and 6.30.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It's alright—I'll come back.

text: I was getting to that bit.

text: In case Michaelia misses me, I'll be back.

text: I'll have to jump in now.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We will take the dinner break from 6.30 to 7.30, as per the agenda, and Minister Wong will return at 7.30. For the purpose of this next block, if we can prioritise the questions for Dr Kennedy, that would be great. We will be running in 10-minute blocks. Senator Hume.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you for appearing, Dr Kennedy, and thank you very much for your opening statement. On 9 September, the Senate passed a cross-party resolution reaffirming its constitutional scrutiny powers and rejecting any attempts of the executive to diminish them. On 13 October, the Senate went further and directed you personally to appear today. Thank you for appearing. Do you accept that answering questions before parliament is part of the job and not an imposition on it? I wonder whether you would be prepared to appear before future estimates hearings.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Certainly, when requested to appear on any matter. I agree that it is definitely part of the job and I would always comply with such a request. The previous practice for people in my position, which I understand began in the late 1970s with Sir Geoffrey Yeend, was that the Secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet usually did not attend estimates. There have been examples when the person in my position has attended since. I'm aware that one of my predecessors, Phil Gaetjens, attended twice. Max Moore-Wilton attended once. I'm not aware of any other of my predecessors attending these meetings. If you had a matter which you thought was serious and you required my attendance, of course I would attend. Otherwise, I would be inclined to follow the longstanding conventions that have been established. I think they've served the process well, but, of course, these are matters for the Senate, not matters for me to determine.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
