text: I just want to be really clear. Has the Secretaries Board discussed this issue since the Senate's order was made?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes. I chaired the Secretaries Board in Dr Kennedy's absence last week. The discussion went to the fact that Dr Kennedy had been invited today to appear. There was no substantive discussion about the question of consent that you're referring to.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
Can I make a few points that I think are relevant to this. If you read the submission itself, it is very clear that the Secretaries Board support parliamentary accountability and recognise the roles and responsibilities of public servants in relation to committees. The submission states inter alia:

The Board's concern is not robust questioning itself. Strong scrutiny is both legitimate and necessary. The concern arises only where conduct crosses the line into behaviour that demeans, intimidates, humiliates or personally targets Official Witnesses.

They also make comment about 'excerpts of committee proceedings on social media where the material is presented without context and exposes officials to ridicule, hostility or abuse.' I would also draw your attention to page 4 of the submission. I think some of what people are being called on social media after excerpts of videos from committees are posted is particularly relevant.

I don't think we should be facilitating people being called—I am hesitant to repeat some of the words that are here. I don't think we should be participating in that. So I think there is a reasonable question about parliamentarians recognising the roles that public servants play and recognising the way in which they can become targets on social media. The submission goes on to talk about agencies being required to conduct insider threat assessments in response to these circumstances.

Now, I know there was a very strong political response from the Australian Greens, from Senator Shoebridge, from Senator David Pocock, from Senator Cash, and I understand why that occurred. But I would also encourage us to think about the wellbeing and safety of some of the people who we question. I think that's what the board submission is about. I don't think it is about the secretaries—how I read it and how I've heard Dr Kennedy today—avoiding their accountability to the parliament.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Senator Hume, we will rotate the call. If you had a final—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I have more questions.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, I'm well aware. I'll just keep circulating round if that's okay. Finished on that section? Senator Pocock.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm sitting here thinking about a time that I did cut a series of responses from the head of the Bureau of Meteorology. I don't know if you ever saw it, but all I did was take every example of 'I will take this on notice', and then the secretary turned—he hadn't brought anyone with him. He turned to a vacant room. It was definitely ridiculous, and he was exposed to ridicule, but, in my opinion—and this is the thing: it's an opinion, and you don't want to be the arbiter. What you think is ridiculous—or what has been misused—will be different, possibly, from what I think. But I think the Australian public deserved to see what an extremely highly paid, senior public servant, who was spending well over a billion dollars, had come to estimates unprepared to respond to. I think the Australian public needed to see that. That's my opinion. I want to hear your response to that, Secretary, because I think—yes, it was cut, and it did expose that person to ridicule, but I think it was in the public interest, and I think there's a place for that.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I guess my view would be—I won't comment on the specific case. I don't know it; I'm sorry. I haven't seen your clip. If it's fair and accurate reporting of what occurred—of course. And it's a matter for you; it's not a matter for that official, in any way, to determine how that should subsequently be presented. And, if some circumstance shows that an official has not met their requirements—I'm not commenting on this specific case—
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I hear that.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
and people have that type of reaction, that is fair and accurate reporting. That is not what we're arguing against here.

And I think, just to go to the issue of the CEOs of agencies, or secretaries, we certainly—if I could just draw a slight distinction—understand our full accountability for our organisations. The buck stops with us. There's no doubt about that. Some of my colleagues have drawn examples to where much less senior officials appearing are feeling under considerable pressure and perhaps are a little less hardened by the exercise. And, really, it's the senior official that is accountable, ultimately. It is that CEO—or me, in this case, for Prime Minister and Cabinet. And so, perhaps, I guess, my only reflection would be that you're absolutely right to focus the approach on the person who is fully accountable, and, where it's clear that the answers—public officials have an obligation to be prepared to answer questions when they come to this place. I was watching the session before me and watching my colleagues from the NIAA answering questions about grants and programs. It's exactly the type of thing an official needs to be in place to do, and all I can say is it's a reasonable expectation. I can't comment on the specific example, but I don't—if we have not performed our duties and people think we look ridiculous, then that's what is deserved in those circumstances.

We're just, I guess, putting some thoughts forward to that inquiry around parliamentary standards that—we're trying to avoid being pulled into the necessary political arguments that are going to take place across parties. Of course the administration is our responsibility. The policy is the government's responsibility. We will have to serve governments of different persuasions in the future. We're trying to keep the service apolitical. Senator Hume has been one of my ministers. I've worked closely with Senator Cash in the past. Hopefully, they found that experience effective. That is obviously the administration of an official—that you were talking about—and their department. But it is trying to just retain that—we're part of the executive but retaining that separation that sees us as an apolitical service. But administration of these programs and providing answers to your questions that could be reasonably foreseen is absolutely a responsibility of all officials.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Just a quick follow-up—in your commentary today, you have referred to asking for the removal of abusive or harmful responses. Have you ever asked for removal and it hasn't occurred? Do you have any knowledge of the refusal to do that?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'll ask Mr Walter to comment on that.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm not aware of any examples, but, really, I think we'd have to check with other departments to see if they'd had that experience.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Our usual experiences have—I've always found my experiences, frankly, to be very respectful and very appropriate. I've appeared in front of you in other capacities, and my understanding—from one of my secretary colleagues, at least—is that there was a very quick reaction when a senator was notified of some offensive material. We drew that out because we're very appreciative of that action, and we just wanted, perhaps, to put it on the record—that that may be something we might ask of senators more frequently if we observe that type of vile abuse. As the minister said and as all of you would know, this abuse is pretty revolting.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes. Thank you for your answers.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Can I finish that block, or are we going to—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm just going to rotate around, because you'll be left with very little. You'd have, like, three minutes if you wanted to take it.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes. I could probably do it within three minutes.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay, go.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Just following on from Senator Pocock's comments, the question of who that arbiter would be is something that I'm struggling to understand. Who is the arbiter of whether something is mischaracterising proceedings or not?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It's the parliament.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, okay. And is this—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: When I read this—and I only read it when it was reported, just to be clear—I thought I could see what the secretaries were seeking to grapple with. I think, Senator Barbara Pocock, you referenced public interest, and I think that is relevant, because you've spent a lot of your life, as I have, arguing for safe workplaces for people, and I know that that is one of the things that the secretaries are talking about. But we also believe in accountability, as you said, to the public and the important role in our democracy that Senate estimates plays, and I do think that. But, ultimately, it's up to parliamentarians to both determine and act in accordance with the standard they think is appropriate.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, and, look, to draw on examples, yes, I've seen the vitriol of people on social media jumping on, commenting, posting. My staff spend an enormous amount of time moderating to remove negative comments. I suppose it's more than a full-time job—moderating comments on social media these days. But I suppose I don't quite—the media can still clip and share videos, and that feedback loop continues. Can I just clarify: is your proposal limited to public servants? Were you intending to extend it to ministers?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We were reflecting on our experience as public servants in these inquiries. Your guidelines go to the behaviour of parliamentarians with all people who attend not only Senate estimates committees but other committee hearings. We were just putting forward some ideas for the joint committee to consider for the guidelines it provides back to parliamentarians about the treatment of officials but also official witnesses more broadly. I fully accept that more broadly there are plenty of people out there who are going to cut around all this stuff, make a vile post and get vile comments. I'm not silly. What we're trying to do is ensure that we keep these good, respectful relationships and that we have these very productive engagements with senators as they robustly inquire into our administration of programs. You had, sensibly, guidelines developed—I think in 2024—that go to these issues. We thought they were good. You were having an inquiry into it, and we thought there might be some helpful ways to think about those guidelines, but, as the senator said, they're entirely matters for you. I've been coming to estimates for well over 20 years, and some of my colleagues have too, and we were hoping this would help and continue what is we think very robust and productive engagement. But social media has brought a new dimension to it. We have particularly more junior officials, if you like, who have been somewhat affected by their treatment.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, it's that line between legitimate critique and what is a misleading clip. That's something I think we need to be very conscious of.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We completely understand—
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm sorry, my time is up.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We completely understand and assert no role in that process. We just bring it to your attention.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We'll go to Senator Payman.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
Good afternoon. Last estimates I asked a question on notice about the cabinet seating plan, which received this response:

Consistent with longstanding practice, the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet does not disclose information about the business and operations of cabinet.

In responding to a question asked under the previous Labor government, the department broke this longstanding practice and provided an outline of where cabinet ministers sit when the cabinet meets. My question is: when did this 'longstanding practice' come into existence? Sixteen years ago it didn't exist.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'll ask my colleague Pauline to come to the table and take that for you. She would have prepared the response.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I am not aware of the seating plan having previously been released.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I've got it in question PM 11 18 October 2010.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: There you go!

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I can circulate it, if you would like.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I think the answer is the answer as you've read out.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: How long does a practice have to stand before it becomes longstanding?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That's probably asking for an opinion, but certainly, since I have been in this role, my understanding is that matters relating to the business and operations of cabinet aren't released. That does include seating plans. I'm not sure what occurred in 2010. I wasn't in this role then. As far as I know, no other—
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Secretary, are you able to comment on that?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No, I'm not aware of what occurred. I haven't followed the seating plan debate to be honest with you.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm curious as to why PM&C were able to identify who sat where in cabinet 16 years ago but not this year. The issue isn't where in cabinet people sit, but it's concerning that it's not even up for discussion. For something as benign as the seating arrangement, why is that being obfuscated from being discussed?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I think Pauline has given you the answer that's been prepared in consultation with the government.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Does PM&C believe this conduct assists with providing 'the freest possible flow of information' to the parliament, as set out in the PM&C guidelines for official witnesses?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Sorry; what was that again?
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Is this conduct of not having the information available or being willing to discuss it in accordance with the PM&C guidelines for official witnesses, which basically asks for 'the freest possible flow' of information to parliament?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: You asked the question on notice; we answered. That answer is based on my knowledge and also our longstanding understanding of what has previously occurred. In terms of the free flow of information, I'm happy to answer any questions that I can answer to the extent that I can answer them.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Even though I've given an example that shows it's not really longstanding practice—but I've got another example. To another question where I asked for the number of times the National Security Committee of cabinet met in recent years, the response referred to a previous answer which noted the same longstanding practice of nondisclosure on cabinet matters. In responding to a question under the Gillard government, the department broke with this longstanding practice to identify that the NSC met eight times to date in 2011 and 21 times in 2010. The 2011 answer notes that the government publicly reports the number of cabinet and committee meetings on an annual basis. Was this a longstanding practice, and, if so, when was that longstanding practice replaced with a new longstanding practice which is the opposite of the previous longstanding practice?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Once again, I'm not aware of the circumstances in which that question was answered. We have made comments before, here at estimates, that we're—a good example was after the Bondi incident. The Prime Minister has done press conferences where he has talked about the NSC having just met. Because he has disclosed it and he is chair of the committee, we may count those up. But, if it hasn't been disclosed by the Prime Minister, it is standard practice not to disclose the number of committee meetings.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So is it standard practice or longstanding?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I do not know what the circumstances were for the answering of the question in 2010 and in 2011.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay. Well, for your officials who may note this, the question is PM24, 15 April 2011. I'll raise more examples on notice, because we could be here all day. But, more generally, the responses to these questions, I feel, not only serve as an indicator of this government's addiction to secrecy and the increasing politicisation of the public service but also represent a decline in the department's ability to respond to questions on notice, compared to years prior. Would you say the PM&C is a department of diminished capability?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: You're asking me for a comment. Given you're commenting on my area, I'd prefer to say that we're not an area of diminished capability.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So how would you explain why the department cannot answer these questions, which it was previously able to?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I don't think it's fair to go to capability in these circumstances—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I think—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I hadn't finished. If it's okay, let me just finish my answer, and then you can ask a question. The officer has given the answer about why the government is not providing information in relation to the number of National Security Committee meetings. You may not agree with it. You're entitled to not agree with it. But I think that goes to the capability—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I don't think it is—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: If you don't agree with it, that's fine. But that's not an issue of the capability of the department; it's a case of having a different position.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I think Ms Sullivan said that she is not aware of why the longstanding practice 16 years ago, back in 2010, took place. She basically just said that that's not something that the current government does. So I'm just trying to understand why it was the case 16 years ago but no longer is the case now. I was hoping that Dr Kennedy could shed light, given his years of experience in this position. But we'll leave it at that. Thank you.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We'll go to Senator Hume.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Back to the Secretaries Board submission, on page 7 of the submission, under 'Strengthened Chair Responsibilities', the submission asks parliament to consider allowing chairs to refuse senators the call and giving them the powers to remove parliamentarians. With full respect to the chair that we have at this estimates hearing, the chair is ordinarily a government senator. So I find it quite confronting that the head of the Public Service is proposing that a government chair should have the ability to remove an opposition senator from questioning an official or a secretary too robustly. Is that what this is saying?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
No, that's not what it's saying. If you read that full paragraph, it says:

The committee may also wish to consider if there is value in giving the chairs powers to remove parliamentarians participating in committees who have acted inappropriately.

Of course, it's a matter for the parliament to determine that standard, which you've done through the standards and the code. It then goes on:

Of course, this should only be used where other approaches have failed.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The standards and the code, obviously, are things that are relevant outside of the chamber, and a committee inquiry is a subset of the chamber, really. So I'm not entirely sure how that works.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm sorry, I don't think I quite understand that.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Sorry, Chair; I don't understand the question.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: You've said that this is for 'committee members who engage in behaviour that is inconsistent with the behaviour standards and the behaviour code', but the behaviour standards and the behaviour code are irrelevant to behaviour outside of the chamber. This is a subset of the chamber. A committee is a subset of the chamber. Parliamentary privilege is paramount here.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, I don't disagree with that. I think what we're saying is where you've got—I was using that as an example. The secretaries are concerned about two things. One is the one we've talked about a fair bit, which is social media. But the other is in relation to the conduct of some parliamentarians—those who appear before committees—and where behaviour is abusive or it's bullying or it's otherwise inappropriate in a parliamentary sense or in terms of the control of the committee. That's the type of circumstance the secretaries were concerned about, and—it's a question mark; this whole thing is a question mark for the committee—whether there should be greater powers for committee chairs to deal with that kind of egregious behaviour.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: A committee chair has the same power as the President of the Senate in this room—yes? So I think they've already got whatever powers the President of the Senate would have.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm not going to fight with you over Senate powers. You would know them much better than I would. But we're trying to say: should there be better guidance or instructions for chairs on how to do that?
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Obviously, you didn't consult the Clerk of the Senate before this document was prepared. We know that because the Clerk, when asked about it, suggested that perhaps—and I'm putting words into his mouth here—it was an overreach on behalf of the Secretaries Board. Can I ask whether you received any legal advice whatsoever on this, whether it was from the Australian Government Solicitor or anybody else, before you decided to submit this document.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The department did not seek legal advice in relation to the submission, but it was broadly consulted across government.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The submission identifies accusations of 'hiding' information, 'covering up' for the government and 'being a liar' among the conduct that it wants addressed. I'm interested in the board's position that a senator should never be able to put to an official that the evidence that they're giving is untrue.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That's not our position, Senator. Of course, if a senator believes that an official—it's a very serious accusation—is lying or doing something along those lines, then you have an obligation to address those issues. Once again, perhaps we could have worded it more effectively. We're just encouraging people to consider not using that type of language in an easy, ongoing manner. But of course, if you felt that any particular official was lying, you have obligations to address that issue. We're not saying it can never be used. We're just concerned that we're seeing a pattern of use.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: If a senator believes that an official has misled a committee, how does the board propose that they test that evidence?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: If a senator truly believes they have misled the committee, then of course they should raise it. That's part of robust—it can be robust and vigorous, and you have those obligations. We're not suggesting in any way that you wouldn't pursue an official who you thought was misleading the Senate in any way.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Well, there's no standing order that would prevent them from doing that, certainly.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We're in furious agreement about what your proper powers and obligations are, and you should pursue them to the fullest extent as you see fit. We were providing some ideas for this committee to consider how best to do that in a respectful way and for us to be able to have the type of conversation we're having today rather than—it's not a pattern I've personally experienced, but certainly some of my colleagues have seen a different tone at times, and we're just encouraging the more productive type of tone that we're having today.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I suppose there is a grey area here. It is an understanding—and perhaps you can clarify this for me—that departmental officials have potentially spent time with consultants or had training as to how they present their evidence to committees. Are you aware of any time that there has been training as to how to present evidence in a particular light? Has there been anybody hired to assist officials with presenting their evidence?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The Australian Public Service Commission has training for officials who are going to appear in front of committees, because they need to be, as I was discussing with Senator Pocock, fully aware of their responsibilities under the guidelines. They have to be ready and prepared to answer questions and respond to senators who are seeking information in a more concise way, for example. So that training is offered particularly to junior public servants. I'm not aware of and would be very concerned if there were any examples of any training going on that was trying to help officials deliberately conceal information. That would be not only concerning but also illegal.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Can I add something? I think the conduct that the secretaries were concerned about is when robust questioning which could go to accuracy or the details of a program or policy turns into personal attacks on the public servant. Absolutely test the validity of what is being said, but then there seems to be in some of the examples we saw this easy jump to 'You're lying,' 'You're deliberately misleading.' It then becomes a 'You are a liar,' 'You have no morals.' That type of character attack or character insinuation—I withdraw the word 'attack'—that secretaries were concerned about. It is less the robust questioning of whether we were getting it right or giving you the information that you were looking for.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We do understand, effectively, the inquisitorial-style powers that you have as senators and the appropriate role you have in inquiring into the Public Service and its administration. As you said, there are judgements to be made and a grey zone in which you are operating, and you have that overriding responsibility to the public in the broad to pursue these things. We're not in any way trying to diminish that. We're actually trying to promote the most productive way that could occur and the most productive way an apolitical service could respond to those types of inquiries. But this is not to in any way diminish—and I know you well—your ongoing appropriate desire to pursue those matters as far as they should be pursued. There's no attempt to diminish that in any way.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: With all of the evidence that you've given today and the response that you've seen from the Clerk and from the Senate to the submission that you've made to the standards committee, I'm wondering: had you had your time over again, had the Secretaries Board had its time over again, would this document have had some legal advice? Would it would you have sought legal advice before it was submitted? Would you have worded it differently? Would you take the opportunity now to rewrite it and perhaps resubmit it to the standards committee?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm not concerned about its legal foundation, but Mr Walter may wish to respond. But the Secretaries Board thought this inquiry was the best way to raise the issues, because it was an inquiry into those standards. We were mindful of ensuring that the views were clearly seen as coming from us. A few secretaries—I won't say a number—have written at times to chairs, I believe, raising these issues in the past, so I don't think they will be completely novel to the Senate or the Clerk, I hope. There's possibly a little bit of conflation between what the Secretaries Board did and the experience of Ms Perkins when she appeared at the inquiry.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Because that was exactly what she was referring to—the Secretaries Board submission.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
She was using some of the language that we spoke about and that I mentioned earlier—on consent or the use in social media of people's image outside of the framework of parliament. That's a matter for Secretary Quinn and Ms Perkins to address in their inquiry. All I would encourage as you look through—I actually thought the Clerk's response was to that evidence rather than the secretary's submission, but I may have misunderstood that. I thought that was what his evidence was about.

We can always think of better ways to do things, but we thought it was best, rather than sitting quietly in a room, not talking to you about it, that we use an inquiry process to bring issues forward and have, hopefully, a constructive debate, raising the issues and trying to improve the operations of the Senate. And so I don't regret at all working with the secretaries to bring forward the issues, but I also don't claim to be perfect in every way in bringing those issues forward.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: When does the Secretaries Board next meet?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We met last week, so it'll be in three weeks time.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: At last week's meeting, was this issue raised?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I think Mr Giffords already answered that, just saying that there was a brief discussion about it, noting that Dr Kennedy had been called to this hearing.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: At the next Secretaries Board meeting, will this issue be raised again? Would the Secretaries Board take that opportunity to potentially rewrite its submission or adjust its submission so that it might withdraw or amend those recommendations that clearly the Senate is going to reject?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I don't think we will rewrite or withdraw our submission. It was to the committee, and it's up to the committee. The committee can of course choose to reject any of the suggestions we made around guidance. That is now on the record. We actually provided a couple of options in the suggestions that we made to, as I said, try and encourage an open debate. I can check with my colleagues if you like, but I don't think any of my colleagues would resile from the importance of raising these issues with you even if, in your view, they weren't raised in the most constructive way. I will say, having been a secretary now for nearly nine years, that these issues have been present for quite some time and perhaps have been increasing over time. And so the inquiry and, we thought, the very positive steps taken by parliamentarians around these standards looked to us to be a good opportunity to make a make the contribution. My preference would be to leave it at that. As you've said, it's not a matter for us; it's a matter for parliament. We've made our submission. The committee can choose to reject the advice and take it no further. That's entirely a matter for you and that's entirely appropriate. I'd probably leave it there.
witness_organisation: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you. I think that the Senate has made it very clear that it's going to re-assert its constitutional authority, but I understand that.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Well, if I could just be clear—if you don't mind me responding, Chair—I said in my opening statement that we agreed with everything you said. text: Okay. I understand you're quite expert in these matters. agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you, Dr Kennedy, and thank you, Senator. In relation to measures for future resilience and trying to reduce Australia's dependence on fossil fuels, which are imported mostly, there are a number of programs that have been announced. In particular, there is the $1.1 billion Cleaner Fuels Program to establish a domestic low-carbon liquid fuels industry; the $55 million to deliver the Transport Resilience and Capacity Kickstart program to incentivise increased freight volumes by rail and maritime transport—a mode-shift piece; and $40.5 million to accelerate the electrification of Australia Post's delivery fleet. So there have been measures that work across looking to future resilience—not just increasing stores and availability of fossil fuels and putting Australia in a more secure position on that front but thinking about measures of how we can reduce our reliance on fossil fuels altogether.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: While you're looking for those, recognising that Dr Kennedy will be leaving shortly, Dr Kennedy, can I ask you to talk about what diesel imports mean for persistent inflation and the terms of trade. Is that something you can reflect on today, to make the most of your time with us?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
It's certainly a good question to send to Secretary Wilkinson of the Treasury, but, given my previous experience, I can reflect on that. In broad terms, depending on the nature of an energy shock, sometimes the terms of trade can rise in Australia if it's a broad demand for energy, because, obviously, we remain a very significant thermal coal and gas exporter, and, if those things are part of the same energy shock, then Australia benefits in the sense that we benefit from the terms of trade. If it's particularly narrowly focused on that fuel itself and we're not getting a broader, if you like, energy price increase, then, all other things given, it would be a negative for the terms of trade, so it would reduce national income in the broad. It very much depends on the nature of the shock and how it spreads.

Most energy shocks spread pretty quickly because people are substituting alternative energy sources. If there's one source of energy that is experiencing an acute shortage, it tends to quickly flow into others. In fact, while we haven't seen it in Australia, gas prices have risen in other parts of the world as a result, for example, of the issues in the Middle East. Sadly, economics is a lot like this. It depends.

In summary, a narrow shock just on that liquid fuel and not affecting other forms of energy would, I would say, be a negative for the terms of trade. The more usual circumstance is it broadly raises energy prices, and, as a broader energy producer, Australia could benefit. I hope that helps.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: If you like, I can start back a couple of steps. The role of Prime Minister and Cabinet, through the caretaker period or the election period, was to collate or pull together all of the election commitments made by parties and individuals into a comprehensive list. I think my colleague went through this at the rural and regional committee last week. That list is then shared, as a normal process, with the government, when they form government. That occurred in the context of the May 2025 election. That list, at that point in time, just after the election, I would deem an initial list. That's the best list at that time, which goes to an understanding of the government's set election commitments and what Prime Minister and Cabinet has collated. Then there's a process undertaken by government, normally through a budget process, of authorising or giving the policy framing or the policy authority for those commitments. Prime Minister and Cabinet, throughout that process, works with relevant portfolio departments in terms of which of those commitments should be implemented by which department. So, in this context, yes, those were the major and local infrastructure projects that went to the department of infrastructure. I hope that helps with the broader setting and the role of PM&C.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: As Mr Exell said, post-election there's a process of basically doing a quality assurance on the commitments. It's also worth noting that, during election campaigns, PM&C has a role in tracking election commitments, and that's across—as for all departments—all parties who may form government. But also, given our central coordinating role, we track all portfolios. Individual departments track their own portfolio commitments made by various parties. So, once a government has formed, and we then meet with the PMO, we work through what they think has been committed to, in terms of their election commitments. We see how it lines up with ours. Then there's a process where, once we've reconciled those, we then go out to all departments to check against their lists as well. It's basically a reconciliation process. It's also, as I said, a quality assurance process, given that you'll often get duplicates of commitments or things will be categorised incorrectly, or you may even have a commitment made by party X that actually should belong to party Y—that sort of thing. A lot of that process—well, the entire process—is essentially getting agreement on what the commitments are and whether they are in the correct portfolio.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay—very mysterious. I have a question for the Office of Impact Analysis. The Government Guide to Policy Impact Analysis and the OIA's Best Practice Consultation guidance identify 30 to 60 days as a suggested consultation period for significant reforms. Can you just explain to the committee what the basis for that timeframe is? Is it just a recommendation or is it an expectation, that 30 or 60 days is reasonably long and reasonably broad?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you for the question. The impact analysis requirements, where they apply, do ask agencies to address the seven questions which are outlined in the impact analysis framework. That includes outlining the consultation undertaken and how that's being considered within the policy analysis. That's a requirement of the framework. The OIA also provides some best practice guidance on our webpage, which you referred to, which notes that the length of consultation rounds will depend on the nature of the impacts of the proposal, the objective of each round, the number of rounds, the form of consultation and who is being consulted. The consultation period undertaken would be a matter for departments and ministers and would depend on the significance and the complexities of the proposal.

witness_position: Executive Director, Behavioural Economics Team of the Australian Government and Office of Impact Analysis

text: On 1 July this year, there was a change in the framework, so the Office of Impact Analysis no longer provides a formal assessment of the quality of impact analyses. agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian National Audit Office
text:
Thank you. First, on behalf of the ANAO, I want to express our sadness on the deeply distressing events of last week in relation to Dr Helen Haines, and our thoughts and best wishes are with her and her family at this time.

This year, 2026, marks 125 years since the first Commonwealth parliament passed the Audit Act 1901. While much has changed since Federation, the ANAO's purpose remains constant: to provide independent assurance to the parliament and contribute to better outcomes for the Australian public. Our 2025-26 annual report, tabled on 22 September 2026, sets out how we fulfil this enduring purpose through independent, high-quality reporting on the financial and non-financial performance of Australian government entities.

During the year, we delivered 243 audit opinions for annual financial statements of Commonwealth entities and companies, audit opinions for 21 annual performance statements of material Commonwealth entities, 39 performance audits, one priority assurance review—the 2024-25 Major projects report—as well as one other report, on the Australian National University's financial management, and a range of other assurance activities, reports and services to support transparency, accountability and performance in the Australian government sector.

Our audits have reinforced the importance of disciplined governance, effective controls and clear accountability in supporting sound public administration and in delivering value for money. Ninety-six per cent of ANAO performance audit recommendations were agreed to by audited entities and, based on entities' self-reporting, more than 90 per cent of recommendations have been implemented within 24 months of reports being presented, contributing to improved performance.

Our work continues to be shaped by broader trends affecting the Australian public sector. Geopolitical developments, fiscal pressures, the rapid emergence of new technologies—including artificial intelligence and heightened cybersecurity and cyber risks—are among the factors influencing government activity and risk and therefore the ANAO in its work as the government's independent auditor.

We met five of our nine performance measures last year. External pressures, including rising costs and delays in activity by audited entities, contributed to the targets not met. We will continue to focus on aspects of our performance that are within the ANAO's control.

Beyond delivering our mandated functions in 2025-26, we made progress against our strategic priorities related to impact, innovation and our people. In the first year of implementing our strategic program, we trialled new approaches to audits, including rapid reviews and 'report at a glance' plain-English summaries. We better calibrated our audit effort to risk, launched our digital strategy and AI policy and increased use of data analytics and AI tools. We're also increasing our focus on internal staff mobility and career development and streamlining aspects of our governance, and we introduced additional staff engagement activities.

Our work is underpinned by an enduring focus on quality and integrity. At a time when serious ethical breaches in the private audit profession have occurred, we have worked to strengthen the quality and integrity assurances we seek from our contractors as well as continually improve our internal quality and integrity systems. These foundations are essential to maintaining the independence of the office and the trust that's placed in our work by the parliament and the Australian public.

The ANAO reported an operating deficit of $0.768 million, just under $1 million, in 2025-26, reduced from a $6.5 million operating deficit in the previous year. Achieving this improvement required a range of actions to increase efficiency as well as a reduction in our work program—including lowering the target number of performance audits from the longstanding historical target of 48 to a range of 38 to 42 in this past year.

Financial sustainability remains an ongoing priority. In its 2026-27 budget-day statement, the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit observed that funding of the ANAO continues to be of serious concern to the committee as it threatens the robustness of the vital audit function that this agency conducts for the Commonwealth. A benchmarking exercise of the Australasian Council of Auditors-General found that Australia's auditor-general independence arrangements fell from a ranking of fifth in 2009 to ninth in 2025, out of 12 rankings. Low scores on financial and managerial autonomy were key factors contributing to this result.

I'd like to conclude by acknowledging my ANAO team. Our people are the foundation of all that we achieved in 2025-26. Audit is demanding work, and this year we asked a great deal of our auditing staff and those who support them. I'm proud of the ANAO team and grateful for the professionalism, engagement and deep commitment to our purpose that they've shown throughout the year. Thank you and we look forward to answering your questions.

text: Thank you for the questions. I think the first audit that you referred to was an ANAO performance audit that was tabled in June 2024, which found that Services Australia's management of critical cyber incidents was partly effective. Key deficiencies at that time included a lack of a detailed, comprehensive cybersecurity incident management policy, a lack of clear escalation paths or timeframes for reporting major infiltrations to bodies like ASD, and an absence of structured approaches for threat and vulnerability assessments during incidents. At that time, Services Australia accepted all 10 recommendations that the ANAO made. The accountable authority would have received the report as part of our standard process of sending a proposed report before publication. As I said, they accepted all 10 recommendations. The audit was a point in time, and we've not audited implementation, but the recommendations would appear to have relevance to the management of the recent incident in relation to open AI bots accessing the website. text: The reference to vague definitions and unknowns as a challenge in this presentation that was made—it's not an uncommon challenge for auditors, particularly in policies where measurement of outcomes is difficult. As an example, in climate change policy the measurement of scope 3 emissions is a challenge because of definitions and unknowns. text: Thank you very much to the ANAO for joining us today. Sorry for the delay in the timing. I know that you couldn't think of anywhere you'd rather be! I now ask the Department of Finance to come to the table as swiftly as they can.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Welcome, Mr Yannopoulos, the Secretary of the Department of Finance, and other officers from the Department of Finance. We will go to Minister Farrell for an opening statement.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I want to briefly address the devastating events of the past week and the attack on the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines, outside her electorate office in Wangaratta. Our thoughts remain with Helen; her husband, Phil; her children and grandchildren; and her staff, many of whom were present in Helen's moment of need. Helen is rightly described as a true community representative, someone who has always sought consensus and outcomes over any attention or headline. Although investigations are ongoing, it is clear to every member and senator in this place that our institutions are experiencing a surge in threats, violent behaviour and intimidation, particularly fuelled online. I want to particularly acknowledge the many women elected across the parliament who have shared their ongoing experience of vile threats and online abuse. This violent and threatening behaviour is not limited to elected officials and is increasingly experienced across our frontline workers, including emergency services, retail, hospitality, teachers and nurses. Every worker deserves to go home safe, including those elected by their communities. As the Special Minister of State and a lifelong unionist, I hold the safety of our agency officials, elected parliamentarians and their staff as the highest priority. Attacks and intimidation on our parliamentarians, our candidates and our institutions threaten not just the individual but our proud democracy as a whole.

Earlier this year, I established the independent review into the Commonwealth Parliamentary Support System, with safety and security at its core. This reform work has been underway for many months, demonstrating that these growing threats are no surprise to those that work across our democracy. I particularly want to acknowledge the PWSS, IPEA and the Department of Finance who, together with many other agencies, have assisted in our support of Dr Haines and her staff in a difficult time.

I also have the staffing numbers, which I'm happy to provide.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Mr Yannopoulos, do you have an opening statement?

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, I don't.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll go directly to questions. Senator McGrath.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'd like to associate coalition senators with your remarks. Secretary, given the escalating threats against parliamentarians, what specific steps has the Department of Finance taken over the past 12 months to strengthen security arrangements for MP, senators, staff and their families? I acknowledge that the security arrangements are shared with other departments and so forth, but this question is specifically in relation to the Department of Finance.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I will begin, and then my colleague Mr Newnham may wish to add. Over the past period—I don't know whether it's a full 12 months—the government gave us some additional resourcing to do the review of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Support System. Included in that review is an element around security and, in particular, looking at the security of electorate offices. The scope of the Department of Finance and its services to parliamentarians is the Commonwealth parliamentary offices and the electorate offices, as well as the transport arrangements—the car-with-driver service known as COMCAR.

We have been working and we are always responsive to a threat assessment, or a tasking, from either the AFP or Home Affairs, which run the Parliamentary Security Coordination Centre. Where there's an ask for something to be upgraded in an electorate office, we go about that as quickly as possible. Indeed, from the discussions that occurred last week, there are nine different offices that were raised, and we are doing work in those.

Another aspect of your question, Senator, was private residences.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: I suppose families, as such. Maybe that does take in private residences, yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: At this stage, there is not scope within the parliamentary business resources for the Department of Finance to act beyond the premises that I mentioned: Commonwealth parliamentary offices, electorate offices, satellite offices. We do not have legislative support to operate in a parliamentarian's private residence.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: You sort of touched on this, but when were the minimum physical security standards for electorate offices last reviewed?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'll take a step back. I know you're asking about the most recent iteration. That was April of this year, but these are standards that have been in place since 2015. Over the course of those 11 years, there have been a number of iterations and updates to those guidelines. As you'd appreciate, they have multiple components. They can have disability access updates, WHS updates, and, of course in the evolving security landscape, there have been a series of updates to the physical security requirements from a security point of view.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: Secretary, you mentioned nine offices out of discussions last week have requested additional security, if I heard it correctly. How many requests for additional electorate office security measures has Finance received over the past 12 months?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We would need to take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's fine. How many of those requests may remain outstanding, and what is the time between each request being received and the approved security measures being installed? On notice is fine. This is a bit of a dorothy dixer in a way: what is the division of responsibility between Finance, Home Affairs and the AFP for assessing security risks, approving additional protections and then funding them in relation to MPs and electorate offices and, I suppose, residences where that has been required?

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I'll try and articulate this as best I'm able. The Department of Home Affairs provides residential security supports for high office holders and parliamentarians deemed at risk by the AFP. They provide physical security advice to my department as it relates to electorate offices and Commonwealth parliamentary offices, and Home Affairs is responsible for the protective security coordination centre. If you like, that is the organising coordination construct across Home Affairs, Finance, ASIO and the Australian Federal Police.

The AFP have a security protection diplomatic liaison, which is the primary point of contact for parliamentarians for security advice or incident reporting. The AFP conducts investigations, undertakes and maintains threat assessments where required—the AFP is the authority for a threat assessment—and allocates resources according to event based security assessment methodology, for example, close personal protection, uniformed police patrolling and static guarding. As I alluded to in my first answer, we provide secure office accommodation for federal parliamentarians; manage the car and driver services, or Comcar; and we do security clearance administration for members of parliament's staff.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: I appreciate security is part of the review that's been undertaken, but how do the three different agencies coordinate intelligence—is there a committee of relevant classified officers from the three areas that meets to go, 'Parliamentarian X has had a threat against them, therefore, AFP, you need to X, Home Affairs, you need to do Y, and Finance, you need to do Z.' How does it happen; that's what I'm asking. How's the sausage made?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'll ask Simon, but there is an established governance process.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text:
Thank you for the question. Let me start with two overarching points. The first is that there's a protective security framework that applies for all parliamentarians. I know that, at times, the commentary can differentiate between various levels of parliamentarians and so forth, but that framework exists across the entirety of the Australian parliament, and that shapes and frames every scenario that is thrown up about an individual parliamentarian. In other words, threat, vulnerability and risk are assessed through that framework.

The second point I'd make is that how those agencies convene is through the Protective Security Coordination Centre. It is Home Affairs led, but all of the agencies you would expect to be involved are—security agencies, intelligence agencies, operational agencies. So the framework applies to those scenarios. That convening body brings together those entities at least fortnightly, and decisions are taken then, based on the data that's put into that group about the types of actions that need to be taken in relation to a particular parliamentarian. For example, the Federal Police might bring to the table an increased threat level for an individual or a specific threat by one perpetrator against a particular parliamentarian. Finance might bring to the table that, in fact, there's been a series of damages to the electorate office. Others may bring to the table that local, state and territory police have been involved in a number of incidents. And—I'm giving these as examples—from that, the framework is applied, and a series of steps are then taken and recommended. One of those, of course, can be the hardening of security settings in various forums. It might be in their transport arrangements, it might be in their home and residential arrangements, it might be in their personal arrangements and, of course, from a Finance perspective, it might be at their electorate office. Out of that comes, as I said, a series of recommendations, and it is on Finance to implement those security settings.

I'll just, while I've got the floor, say one more thing. Even before you get to those settings, every single electorate office in Australia has standard security settings, right now—before, or despite, individual data points coming in about individual threats to parliamentarians. And, whilst I can't go into the totality of those elements, they include things like closed circuit TV and duress alarms and security alarms and reception barrier hardening, for example. I suppose I just wanted to put that on the committee's radar—that that exists, and there is calibration and scaling according to additional information that comes in to the Federal Police or ASIO or Finance et cetera.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I appreciate that, and I realise, following last week's horrific attack, this will be an ongoing discussion as to how we as a parliament can come forward, working through the government, to ensure that our staff and families and parliamentarians are appropriately looked after.
