text: But, as a backbencher of the Labor Party, she has two additional staffers that other backbenchers—regardless, actually, of their political affiliation—don't receive. Does the Prime Minister think that's fair?

agency: Department of Finance
text: What you've just said is not entirely accurate. There are other backbenchers who have more than the five allocated staff, so there are some others who have that number. Unfortunately, I've given away my copies of the—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Don't give it to him! They have specific roles. Where I'm coming from—and I'll proceed to Senator Payman now, through you, Chair—is that it's a matter of equity of treating like with like and that we have a government backbencher who has two additional staff with no additional roles.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The alternative would have been for Senator Tyrrell to have to terminate those two employees, and I have to say, in the circumstances, I think the Prime Minister made the right decision.

agency: Department of Finance
text: What was the Prime Minister's decision?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It was the Prime Minister's decision to allow her to keep the two appointments that she had previously made.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Payman.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I'll start from the top, because the question is around what's fair and equitable. Nearly two years ago—23 months ago, to be exact—you were asked questions about personal staffing allocations by former senator Birmingham. You said then:

To my knowledge, a request was made by Senator Payman and at least one other senator for additional staff. Again, to the best of my knowledge, the Prime Minister is considering that application.

Is there any legal requirement for the Prime Minister to process these requests in a fair or equitable way?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't think there's any legal obligation.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Sorry, was that, 'There isn't a legal obligation'?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'll get that checked for you, hopefully while we're sitting here, but I'm not aware of a legal obligation to—I mean, he has the legal power to make the determinations, but I don't think there's a legal obligation on him to do it. So he's got the power, but he doesn't have to exercise that power—that is the way I understand it. Unless there's somebody—

agency: Department of Finance
text: We would agree with that. The Prime Minister has the authority to make—
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's at his discretion, yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Right, but there's no requirement under the legislation, as in the way you phrased it.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: Has my request been processed by the Prime Minister?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't believe so.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Do we know why, especially since it's been two years and nothing's happened? Can we explain why this could be?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's an issue for the Prime Minister. I'm happy to raise it with him again and find out what his current disposition is and come back to you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've been waiting for a while, and I've raised this on multiple occasions to you as the Special Minister of State.

agency: Department of Finance
text: And I'm happy to raise it with the Prime Minister.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I note that since you were asked about this, requests for a process were made for the member for Bradfield, who was elected in 2025; for Senator Waters, upon her becoming leader of the Greens; and for Senator Shoebridge, who became leader of the Greens less than a month ago, and determinations were made within a fortnight. Why are some applications being processed in just two weeks and others still awaiting acknowledgement after two years?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That is a question only the Prime Minister could answer, but I'm happy to inquire from him.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Surely, there have to be processes?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm sure the Prime Minister has, as he always does, given it due consideration, and, at this point, has not made a decision to allocate additional staff to you. But I'm happy to go back to him and ask him what his current thinking on it is and to come back to you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you. Ms Nicolette Boele, the member for Bradfield, was elected in 2025. Why is she the only independent in the House of Representatives, apart from the member for Fowler, with one adviser, while all others have two?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't specifically know the answer to that question, Senator Payman, but I will inquire and attempt to come back to you with an answer on that one.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Thorpe, Senator Tyrrell, former senator Vann and the member for Calare all received personal staffing allocations after leaving the political parties under whose banner they were elected. Has the Prime Minister refused to make a decision on my request because, unlike all the other defectors, I defected from the Labor Party?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I will have to ask him.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Am I being made an example of?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'll have to ask him that question and—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Please do, and I'm glad this is on the record because, unlike our private conversations, we can come back to this next time.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Be clear about this Senator Payman: what I say privately is what I say publicly. I don't have—

agency: Department of Finance
text: But I've been waiting for a while, Minister, and you were supposed to talk to the Prime Minister last year before I went on mat leave.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, and I have done so, Senator Payman. But—

agency: Department of Finance
text: So you have spoken to him?

agency: Department of Finance
text: At various times I have raised these—

agency: Department of Finance
text: So what did he say?

agency: Department of Finance
text: He hasn't yet given a response to your request—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Were any reasons given?

agency: Department of Finance
text: —but I'm happy to—I beg your pardon?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Has the Prime Minister given any reasons? Surely, you've raised it on multiple—

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, he hasn't given me reasons, but you've raised it again.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've been raising it for two years, and there are psychosocial hazards that are imposed on my staff because I and my staff are expected to do the job of an office that has seven full-timers. I don't know how the same job, same pay thing that Labor keeps bragging about applies to my team, when my chief of staff is being paid an electorate officer C wage but she's expected to do more work than other independent senators' office chiefs of staff. So please raise this with the Prime Minister. If he cares so much about the welfare and wellbeing of people who work in this building, then I implore you and the Prime Minister to please look into the fact that my staff are burning out. They can't take this any longer. Is the Prime Minister waiting for something like what happened to Dr Helen Haines to occur to my office or to me before he'll take our request seriously?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I personally think that's an outrageous suggestion, Senator Payman.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. I can't believe that I'm saying that or making that suggestion, because it's been two years.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Alright. Then can I—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Payman, I suggest that taking a moment to think about those kinds of accusations while we rotate the call might be a worthy pursuit. We'll go back to Senator—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Can I—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think everyone can make their own—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Chair, can I suggest that Senator Payman go further and withdraw that suggestion about the Prime Minister's motivation, because it's absolutely not the case—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'd love to have a response from the Prime Minister, and then I'll withdraw it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's not what I'm requesting. I'm requesting that you withdraw.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm not withdrawing anything.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Payman, that was quite an outrageous statement. I would ask you to withdraw it. I appreciate your frustration—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Chair.

agency: Department of Finance
text: but I'm not sure that conflating those two issues—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Chair, with all due respect, I haven't made any accusation.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think you just did.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It wasn't. You can take it as an accusation, Minister—

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, I don't want to repeat it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: but once you've discussed it with the Prime Minister, if he thinks that's an accusation, then I'll withdraw it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It'll be too late by then, because, when this session is over, it's too late for you to withdraw.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've been waiting two years, Chair, and I am tired of looking in my staff's eyes and saying, 'You just have to deal with this, because the Prime Minister is petty and is taking it out on me.'

agency: Department of Finance
text: Alright. Senator Payman—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Alright?

agency: Department of Finance
text: These are unparliamentary accusations that you're throwing around, and I would ask you to consider—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Perhaps you could raise it with the President.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I would be delighted to raise it with the President, yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: But such accusations are not within the bounds of parliamentary behaviour. I appreciate your frustration. I really do—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm sorry that it's come to this.

agency: Department of Finance
text: but making those kinds of accusations against another member of the parliament is not where we're at.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You'd expect better.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We should be better than that—

agency: Department of Finance
text: You'd expect from the leader of our country—

agency: Department of Finance
text: and, we thought, particularly on a day like today, we should all be better than that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, absolutely. I agree.

agency: Department of Finance
text: But you're not going to be.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The leader of this country needs to do better.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll go to Senator McGrath.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I do have some other questions in this area, but I might shift just to get an update from the department. I'm pretty sure you know what I'm going to say. Can I get a brief update on the cease and recommence process for MOP(S) Act staff in relation to the concerns I previously raised in this area?

agency: Department of Finance
text:
Yes, Senator. I'm conscious this has been an issue for some time. You've raised it with us for some time. It has taken us longer than we would have liked to solve. What I can say is that we have identified a solution to the cease and recommence issue. Just to remind—there are two main goals here with the rather unique provision for ministerial and parliamentary staff, where they can have a day's break in their employment but receive termination moneys but also need access to the Parliamentary Expenses Management Scheme immediately. It has taken us longer than we would have liked to identify a solution, but that is because it is much more technically complex than first thought. It also challenges the wider integrity of the data capture on that IT platform.

We've identified a solution. It has 16 work packages, if you like, that need to be solved. Recently we had made our way through seven of those, and we have a level of confidence we can solve the remaining nine. After that, we'll undertake a validation process, and that's important because we want to make sure that the users—that is, ministerial and parliamentary staff—see minimal, if any, change to their use of the PEMS system. We also want to make sure, like I said earlier, that making the change in this area does not impact on the data holdings elsewhere and inadvertently cause greater issues than it solves, noting that, of course, the many parliamentary staffers that use this system are joined by thousands of public servants. We don't want to unintentionally disrupt that wider system. So we are working very hard internally and with SAP Australia and SAP India and, as I said, we do believe we have a solution. We're working on getting that in place as soon as possible. It will take us into next year. We are very conscious of having this sorted out as far ahead of the next election as possible, noting that is the sort of surge period where this comes to fruition most prominently.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: On notice I can you provide a date when this could be fixed by. I'm sorry to do that to you, but it's on notice.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's fine, Senator.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: Also on notice, what immediate arrangements are available to ensure affected staff continue receiving their salary while the underlying problem is being resolved. Minister, will you commit to fixing this problem or ensuring the department can fix this problem by a date in 2027?

agency: Department of Finance
text: If you ask nicely, Senator McGrath.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I always ask nicely, Minister, you know that. Please?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay. You've asked nicely then, and I will undertake to fix it. We are an action government, Senator McGrath, and so where we have a problem, we seek to resolve it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Excellent. Before I move on, Minister, can you confirm that Minister Wells had a meeting scheduled with you or your office in Adelaide on 7 June 2025?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. I can confirm that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: What was the purpose of that meeting, who requested it, and when was it arranged?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The nature of the Special Minister of State requires some confidentiality and some privacy. Where members of parliament come to me with particular problems, I respect that privacy, and I respect the fact that they often raise issues of a delicate nature. To the best of my knowledge, every Special Minister of State who I've worked with in this place—we don't discuss the nature of the issues. There are many people on your side of the chamber, Senator McGrath, who come to me with particular problems. I have never once, in the five years I've been in this job, broken the privacy of their issues, and I don't intend to start now.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's okay. I want to know if the meeting ran over time and what time it was scheduled for, if you have that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I couldn't tell you that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: If you could take that on notice, that would be great. I will go back to the department. Can I go to the staffing classification review, please.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Can I say this. If I started talking about these sorts of meetings—

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I'm not expecting a comprehensive view of the meetings. I appreciate that you—I don't want to turn this into one of the fireside chats that sometimes we have, but I do have a role to ask questions. You do know that, and sometimes you may deign to answer them—sometimes.

To the department, in relation to the staffing classification review, are you assured that the classification review has been able to fully consider the issues raised during the last enterprise bargaining exercise, which was the reason the review was committed to in the first place?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm happy to begin. I might ask Ms Frazer or Mr Fulton to come back on any specifics as well. As you've said, this was a review commissioned out of the outcomes from the enterprise agreement. It did experience some delays but has been rapidly worked on of late. The review, as you may be aware, has been completed. There were surveys of electorate office staff between May and June this year. There have been a number of results from that that go to the broader range of functions of staff, the autonomy exercised by them et cetera, in a number of findings. I know your question goes to quite a specific component, and I will pass to a colleague in just a moment, but, for the benefit of the committee, the outcomes from the review were certainly discussed in the employee consultative group on multiple occasions, as they also were with unions. We have shared that with the PWSS and with the independent reviewers as well. Obviously, there are steps ahead, in terms of engagement with the Special Minister of State and government consideration, but, on the specific question, I will turn to Mr Fulton and Ms Frazer.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: The terms of reference that were endorsed by the Special Minister of State in November of 2024 were quite definitive, so we've undertaken the review as best we can within the terms of reference that were endorsed.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Business Enabling Services

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you for that. I have lots of questions, but I do want to get to the AEC, so will be putting them on notice. I'm assured that they will be answered on time. Would that be correct?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We will work to try and get those to you on time.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: Minister—in terms of questions on notice?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We shall respond in our usual prompt manner.

agency: Department of Finance
text: And that's what scares me. I'm finished. Well, not finished; I've barely started. AEC, please.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Most certainly. Can I just touch base on whether we believe we're going to get to the parliamentary workplace support or the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't think we are. Release them.

agency: Department of Finance
text: One of the questions earlier from Senator McGrath regarding security upgrades and the time taken and so forth, we've taken that on notice. I would like to note that we're very, very conscious that, whether it be new measures that are recommended for electorate offices or repairs for damage, for example, that's experienced by electorate offices, from time to time we do experience delays. Sometimes they are unavoidable. Sometimes they are areas that we are striving to do better on. But we will answer that question on notice and get that data for you. In the moment that we're in, I did want to underscore that we're very, very conscious of reacting as quickly as we can to get those repairs in place or new measures in place that go to security requirements.
witness_organisation: Department of Finance

agency: Department of Finance
text: I appreciate the work that you and your fellow officers are doing. Thank you very much.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you very much. We appreciate your time. We will now let you go. I would ask the Australian Electoral Commission to beat a speedy path to the table. I will also now advise that we will release the Parliamentary Workplace Support Service, and questions will all be placed on notice. We will also release the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority, and all questions will be placed on notice.

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Welcome, Mr Pope, Electoral Commissioner. I am delighted to have you seen through the end of the night. Would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: No, thank you, Chair.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: We will go directly to questions. Senator McGrath.

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Good evening, Commissioner, to you and your team. With the substantive electoral funding and disclosure reforms commencing in three months time, can you provide an update on the implementation of the reforms? Actually, it's in two months that the reforms commence.

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: It is about two months and four days.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Excellent. Can you provide an update on the implementation of the reforms commencing in two months and four days.

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: I certainly can. I might just say at the outset I'm incredibly proud of the team that have been working on the funding and disclosure reform program. This has been an incredibly complex task that's been given to the AEC, which I think many have described as the most complex legislation in recent history. It is a very short period of time to build a new system and a new process and to bring a large stakeholder cohort on this journey. The most substantive outcome I can update you on is on 18 October we were successful in integrating our new system for funding and disclosure reform so that disclosure donation notices will be able to be electronically lodged as of 1 January 2027. That enhancement and integration of that new system and new capability into the AEC broader ICT architecture went incredibly smoothly. It actually ran ahead of schedule, and the team who have been working on that for many, many months have done an excellent job. We are now in the process of starting to contact entities to onboard them, to get them effectively registered into the system and to get them linked so that they are ready to go on 1 January 2027. But I could provide a lot more detail if you'd like.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: We may, because it is important, and I'm sorry that it's at the end of today. I want to confirm that the new funding and disclosure system is fully operational and available for end-to-end testing by regulated entities?

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Entities have been involved in user-acceptance testing. I will ask the chief operating officer to complement my answer. I want to be careful so we don't misunderstand where we're at. What we have done is put the first module of the system live, which is for donation disclosure notices. There are many other phases that are planned throughout 2027 to add to this system, but that is the first module, and that will be available for entities to electronically upload their donation disclosure notices on 1 January 2027, when the scheme goes live.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: I suppose that's a good way to clarify or to confirm that, in the next two months, in terms of the entire project, what functions will be ready to go or have been available for people to test but will be ready to go on 1 January? And what functions—I don't want to say 'are still under development', but I can't think of a better way of putting it—are still under development and yet to be implemented over 2027, and I'm referring to your answer?

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: I might ask the chief operating officer to complement my answer and correct it if need be.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: What we have launched most recently is our disclosure capability, so what users can currently do is sign in, create and manage accounts, create their draft disclosure notices, save and review those draft disclosure notices and view disclosure activity ahead of the system being launched on 1 January. From 1 January, we will turn the system on so they can actually lodge disclosure notices at that point, and we will then be able to publish them to the transparency register. The additional two capabilities that we will launch over the coming 12 months will be the funding capability—so the payment of administrative assistance funding, the payment of advanced electoral funding—and the registration of political parties and all of the different elements associated with those two significant capabilities. Then what we have for the AEC's regulatory capability are three additional components, which are the compliance, investigation and enforcement capabilities. We also have some technology uplift, which forms another component of the work that we're doing.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Obviously it's a very large and complex program, with not only a complex IT element but also complex stakeholder engagement education awareness, and there are many challenges still ahead that we still need to navigate. We've got a fantastic team, and they are doing their very best. But I'm conscious that—whilst we're off to a great start, this is a fantastic achievement and a great milestone and it's almost a near-miracle if you like—there is much complexity ahead for us in 2027 and into 2028.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: And for the entities—

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: And for the entities that are coming on this journey.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Can you take this on notice: will you be undertaking an advertising campaign? You're obviously engaging with certain stakeholders at the moment in terms of people understanding—because these are quite serious reforms.

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: As you know, we've been engaging very widely. If I can just rip off the top of my head here—14 user groups with 295 attendees, seven virtual engagement sessions with 380 attendees, nine engagement sessions here onsite at Parliament House, 43 one-on-one engagements, videos, interactive walkthroughs of the systems, 11 fact sheets, 23 detailed guidelines, five videos, seven monthly newsletters that have gone to over 3,000 stakeholders and multiple letters to stakeholders. We're doing a lot. But you're pointing to the fact that, outside of the known entities, there are donors out there that need to be alert to particularly the new changed donation threshold. So, yes, we will be doing an advertising campaign, and the chief operating officer has got more detail on that, if you would like. We can provide it on notice.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Probably on notice, because I've got a couple more questions I want to get in before 11 o'clock, so that would be good, please. Can you give an update on the referendum compliance work the AEC has been undertaking, how many audits have been completed and how many are still ongoing.

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: I may well need to take that on notice unless someone can pull that up at their fingertips whilst we're at the table.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: I'm fine with that. What happens when there is an ongoing review but the organisation has ceased to exist? That's probably a hypothetical question, but it has happened.

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: To the extent we can, we would still want to complete that review and satisfy ourselves of the inquiries that we were pursuing.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: On notice, unless you've got the information to hand, how many organisations or individuals have the AEC asked to submit a return relating to the 2025 election, how many ultimately submitted them and how many have not made a submission?

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Just so I'm clear, that's the election return, not the annual return?
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: The election return.

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Okay. Again, we'll take that on notice unless someone can bring that data to my attention in the next few minutes.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Is the Queensland redistribution progressing to schedule, and could you remind me what the dates are, please?

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Yes, it is. The end of this week is the conclusion of the two-week period for comments on suggestions. We got 63 suggestions in the four-week period that suggestions were open. The team will start analysing the suggestions in the comments on suggestions over the coming weeks, and then I'm scheduled to convene and chair the redistribution committee with my fellow committee members at the end of November. We are doing a truncated approach because we're conscious of the timeline. We're meeting on a number of consecutive days to try and work our way through this as expeditiously as we possibly can but obviously not compromising on process or integrity.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: The Queensland redistribution is not due to be finalised until—is it 27 September?

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Well, 22 September 2027 is the determination date, but, just like the three that have concluded, I anticipate we will make the announcement a couple of months prior to that. It's on a fairly similar trajectory to the three that we've concluded, and we made those announcements in July when the determination date was 8 October.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: If an election is called before the determination is gazetted, would that mean that the election is then held on the old boundaries?

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Correct.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: I've got lots of questions, but I'm not going to push the friendship by pushing answers past 11 o'clock, so I'll put the rest on notice. Thank you, Commissioner, to you and your team for coming in.

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: I can also say election returns—we have seven outstanding, which includes donors that we're still working on. That's about normal.
witness_organisation: Australian Electoral Commission

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: Thank you.

agency: Australian Electoral Commission
text: That does conclude today's hearing. Thank you very much to all the witnesses who appeared, to Hansard, to Broadcasting and to our secretariat for their assistance. I now declare this meeting of the Finance and Public Administration Legislation Committee adjourned.
